item.title: New Research Explores Varieties of Purpose and Happiness
item.description:
Happiness

New Research Explores Varieties of Purpose and Happiness

How different forms of purpose relate to age, gender and happiness

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • We focused on seven types of purposes, including religious, accumulative, self-expansive, and transpersonal.
  • Our "purpose-orientation" varies with age. Older people are more likely to have a transpersonal purpose.
  • Types of purpose affect our happiness; an "accumulative" purpose has a negative link with happiness.
Source: flickr/semona

Psychologists have known for decades that a sense of purpose brings significant benefits, both physically and psychologically. People with a strong sense of purpose tend to be healthier, to live for longer, and to suffer from lower levels of stress, depression, and addiction.

However, less attention has been paid to different types of purpose, and their effects. I recently led a research project on this topic at my university. In a new paper published in the Journal of Humanistic Psychology, we report the findings of a survey of 528 people, in which we investigated whether it is possible to identify different types of purpose, and whether they had different effects. We examined how different types of purpose were associated with happiness, age and gender, and found that significant differences did exist.1

Seven Different Types of Purpose

We focused on the following seven different types of purpose (including the absence of purpose):

  • No purpose: A sense that life lacks direction, meaning, or an overarching goal.
  • Survival purpose: Focusing primarily on meeting basic needs such as food, shelter, safety, and security.
  • Religious purpose: Finding direction through religious faith or another established framework of meaning.
  • Personal-accumulative purpose: Pursuing wealth, career success, status, or achievement.
  • Altruistic purpose: Focusing on helping others, reducing suffering, or contributing positively to society.
  • Self-expansive purpose: Seeking personal growth, creativity, learning, fulfillment, and the development of one's potential.
  • Transpersonal purpose: Experiencing purpose as something larger than the individual—something that seems to flow through a person rather than being consciously created by them. This type of purpose is often associated with a "spiritual" orientation.

Our statistical analysis found that this seven-factor model was valid, working much better than treating all forms of purpose as a single dimension. In other words, we found that it is valid to think in terms of these seven forms of purpose.

We found that most people were oriented around one main type of purpose, even if this overlapped with other types. In our general population sample, the most common purpose was self-expansive, followed by altruistic purpose. These two types of purpose often overlapped to some degree, while a "personal-accumulative" purpose tended to be distinct.

Age, Gender, and Happiness

We found some striking results in relation to age. Younger participants, particularly those aged 18–24, reported higher levels of no purpose and personal-accumulative purpose. Older age groups were less oriented around personal-accumulative purpose, while both altruistic and transpersonal purpose increased with age, peaking among participants aged 65–74. In terms of gender, we found that women were more likely to be oriented around a transpersonal and a self-expansive purpose. Perhaps this aligns with previous research showing that women tend to be more focused on spirituality than men.

The most striking findings of our study concerned happiness. Participants who reported no sense of purpose tended to report substantially lower levels of happiness. Survival purpose was also strongly negatively associated with happiness. Transpersonal purpose was strongly associated with happiness. Self-expansive purpose was linked to happiness too, although to a lesser degree. In contrast, personal-accumulative purpose—the pursuit of wealth, career success, status and achievement—was negatively associated with happiness.

The latter findings are significant in that they contradict the standard cultural assumption that happiness stems from achievement, success, and wealth. Our study found that altruism and a transpersonal purpose are much more likely to bring happiness. In other words, making accumulation and achievement the central organising purpose of life does not provide the same psychological benefits as growth, contribution or a sense of connection.

Applying the Findings

Perhaps the biggest lesson from our research is that asking someone simply, "Do you have a purpose?" may not be enough. More useful questions might be: "What kind of purpose guides your life? Are you just trying to survive? Are you following a religious calling? Are you striving for success? Are you oriented toward self-development or helping others and contributing to the world? Or is your purpose more intangible and spontaneous, guided by intuition, or a deep spiritual impulse?"

When considering these questions, we should be aware that some types of purpose are likely to bring higher levels of happiness—specifically, an altruistic, self-expansive, or transpersonal purpose. At the same time, our research suggests that, as we grow older, we will naturally move towards these types of purposes.

To a large extent, purpose is a choice. Apart from survival purpose—which is forced on us by poverty and hardship—we can choose the goals to which we devote our energy and attention. However, our findings imply that the most effective type of purpose is not voluntary. Transpersonal purpose involves a sense that purpose is being uncovered and expressed rather than created. It is a purpose that arises from letting go—not consciously directing our lives, but allowing life to flow through us in a state of trust.

item.title: A Vacation Is Good Medicine
item.description:
Burnout

A Vacation Is Good Medicine

Taking time off is a healthy imperative.

Posted August 31, 2026

Vacations can take place just about anywhere and are individualized experiences. Maybe your best vacation is filled with adventure, thrill-seeking, physical activities, and new experiences. Maybe you'd rather rest on a beach and read for an entire week. Maybe you want to go on a wellness retreat and reset your diet and physical fitness. Maybe you want to unplug from your devices and camp in the middle of nowhere, where no one can contact you. The beauty of vacations is that they can be whatever you want them to be. Happily, vacations are also quite good for us.

Vacations are an important component of employee health and productivity.
Source: Image by Piyapong Saydaung from Pixabay

Taking vacations from work has been shown to provide significant psychological, physical, and cognitive health benefits. Despite this, 46% of Americans who get paid time off from their employer don’t use it all.

Clearly, for a lot of us, taking time off is a hard thing to do. We don’t want to miss work. We feel guilty about leaving our responsibilities behind. Maybe we don’t believe anyone else can do the job as well as we can. Maybe we are concerned our boss will think less of us if we take time off or that an opportunity will be given to someone else if we do not appear to be “all in.” The list of reasons people don’t take vacations is long.

However, the list of benefits of taking regular vacations is also long. Studies have shown that vacations improve overall general health, improve cardiovascular health specifically, decrease exhaustion, improve general well-being, and improve life satisfaction.

For bosses who don’t support employees taking vacation, they should know that vacations have been shown to increase employee engagement, cognitive ability, and creativity and decrease burnout and absenteeism. A refreshed, healthy workforce will always be more productive than a tired, burned out one.

So now that you’ve decided its time for a vacation, is there a formula for the most optimal one for your health and well-being? While not all vacations are the same, there is a rubric to optimize your vacation. And I’m not talking about Tahiti versus your local lake house. For the health benefits, it just matters that you take one. I’m talking about some general rules of the vacation-road.

Before you go

If you are able to wrap up projects and clear out your inbox before you go, you will have an easier time relaxing and detaching from work on vacation. If you are worried about what’s happening with an ongoing project that you have responsibility for, or you’ve left behind 100 unread emails, as examples, you will have a difficult time unwinding and a pile of work waiting for you when you get back. If possible, time your vacation strategically.

Take a trip away from home

There is evidence that the so-called “staycation” is not as powerful (but is still good!) as the traditional vacation. When one takes time off and stays at home, they are more likely to work and less likely to be able to psychologically detach from work.

Be on vacation

This seems self-evident but how many people have you seen “on vacation” who were fully engaged on a work call, meeting, and who were texting people back at the office? One of the reasons that people take vacations is to get a break from work and thus it should come as no surprise that detaching from work and relaxation are considered the two most vital components of effective vacations. Detaching from work means just that. Checking emails, texts and calling in to virtual meetings while “on vacation” is literally the opposite of vacation.

Take time to unwind

Relaxation is a critical component of a vacation and those who incorporate meditation into their vacation experience longer lasting effects of vacation, including increases in mindfulness and well-being, and lower fatigue.

Other variables that affect how powerful vacation is on health

One of the leading variables determining whether or not the effects of vacation last are whether or not your employer supports vacations. While vacations have numerous health benefits for individuals and a number of benefits for the employer, these benefits are longer lived in work places that support employees taking time off and where employees do not feel their job is at risk if they take time off.

Vacation policies of potential employers should be a key variable if you are looking for a job

How potential employers view vacation-taking is definitely something to consider when applying for jobs. And for your health and wellbeing, final decisions about which job offer to take should consider not just how many vacation days you get, but whether or not your potential new employer supports you using them.

Taking vacations is a health behavior that we should all capitalize on when possible. Vacations are powerful health interventions which improve our abilities to do our jobs well.

item.title: AI Getting Boring? You’re Probably Doing It Right
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Getting Boring? You’re Probably Doing It Right

When we begin to normalize AI, our human strengths may improve.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • We have always normalized new technology over time, no matter how innovative.
  • Ultimately, technology may become more transformative as it become less of a novelty and more of a resource.
  • We still need to use human judgment and experience to make decisions, even if AI is giving us more data.

Even though I expect all of us to keep using artificial intelligence (AI) a lot, I do think it might be time to stop talking about it the way we have been. Not because we're fatigued on AI (though some of us might be, totally fair) but because we might be ready to just normalize our AI experience. That's not a bad thing—normalization is what usually happens when you start to rely on something with confidence. You no longer build around the thing. The thing is just part of your life. I don't stop to think about using AI to check something. It's just open in the browser or available via plug-in or built into whatever I'm already doing.

AI will give us more data. Decisions are still up to us.
Source: Sable Flow/Unsplash

The good thing is now I am starting to use AI less, not more. I use it to improve the last 10 percent of my own ideas, instead of asking an open-ended question and getting 20 ideas I'll never use (and seven of which I don't fully understand). That was fun when I first started learning how to create a prompt. Now it's...boring. I don't want AI slop. I want curated answers built off of how I've trained it.

Using AI to expand your strengths won’t feel radical. That’s not a bad thing.

Here is why the boredom might be progress, for all of us: Now AI is following my judgment. It's narrowed down to ideas within parameters built by my actual experience and expertise. If you're old enough to remember when the internet first took off, you might recall that everyone wanted to literally just "surf the web." Now: when is the last time you just randomly checked that Google did, in fact, have the answer to that question? We no longer question the full scope of the tool; we shape it into usefulness that serves us.

In work situations in particular, ideally each team member is evolving in this way on their own. That isn't that radical. All technology has faded into this standard. Calculators don't replace mathematical thinking; they merely facilitate it. Email was revolutionary until spam made us pull back our usage. Zoom was cool until it was the only way we could communicate for over a year. None of that is bad. It rebalanced from excess to a bounded resource.

That said, while normalization is certainly common (we do it even during abnormal situations like in 2020), and almost inevitable, the pace at which you start to manage use of tools is a choice. By now, most of us have been burned by a bad AI response or fatigued by someone else's. But we also don't plan to abandon AI. In fact, we'll use it more. Those who use it to enhance good judgment will probably pull ahead. People who learned to email enough to communicate more effectively (without replying all to everything) likely were read more often. People who began relying on modeling software enough to be convincing, but not overwhelming, probably had their numbers trusted. It's not always about using something the most, but with the right precision that reveals innovation.

AI is giving us more data. But it’s not yet increasing our wisdom.

Learning to use AI to detail general understanding or analyze hard choices could help improve the inputs to human judgment. But it can help most if we keep it on the “boring” data side of the table. For now, we should be slow to rely on it as a substitute for the most complex aspects of human judgment: experience and the wisdom that comes with it, the instinct we each hold that says when to look deeper regardless of appearance, the sensitivity and empathy to recognize consequences that have to be balanced with goals. That has always been a lot to hold. But it means that we will continue to make human-sized mistakes, which are the ones we (mostly) know how to manage. And that’s probably the right kind of boring for all of us.

item.title: When Motherhood Reactivates Unresolved Trauma
item.description:
Trauma

When Motherhood Reactivates Unresolved Trauma

Motherhood can activate old trauma, affecting identity and emotional regulation.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Entering motherhood can expose trauma that was previously managed, processed, or kept outside awareness.
  • The pressures of new motherhood can overwhelm hard-won psychological growth, especially when stressors rise.
  • Understanding trauma triggers can support perinatal mental health and help mothers respond differently.

The recent social discourse around tradwives, or traditional wives, illuminates dimensions of our psyche, including the father complex. The tradwives debate can also pit women against one another by suggesting that being a stay-at-home or working mother is the better choice.

In 2013, 51 percent believed children were better off when the mother stayed home,1 whereas in 2023, 55 percent believed one parent at home was better, with 22 percent favoring the mother at home and 33 percent saying either parent.2 Interestingly, 50 percent of mothers with children under 18 preferred to stay home rather than work outside the home.3 This data sheds light on the tradwives discussion. However, arguing that one choice is superior neglects the reality of motherhood: It’s difficult no matter what form it takes.

Fifteen years ago, I started “Mentoring Mothers,” which offers consultation and connection for mothers as they transition to a more conscious experience of motherhood. I did so because perinatal mental health support is severely lacking.

The specific link between trauma and motherhood is often neglected.4 There are different kinds of trauma. Colloquially, what are sometimes called “Capital T traumas” generally involve experiencing, witnessing, or learning about a loved one’s death or threatened death; serious injury; or physical, sexual, emotional, or verbal abuse or violence. Capital T traumas can also include life-altering experiences such as natural disasters, famine, human trafficking, war, gang violence, immigration, becoming a refugee, neglect, disease, and medical procedures.

Alternatively, what are often dubbed the “lowercase t traumas” are also damaging sources of psychological pain that may set the stage for more severe pathology, including “complex trauma” or “complex posttraumatic stress disorder,” which is common clinically yet not recognized in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders. These traumas are related to repeated and chronic relational, developmental, and cultural experiences such as discrimination, rejection, abandonment, dismissiveness, and intrusiveness.

Trauma is both deeply personal and universal across culture, time, and history. From a Jungian perspective, trauma and complex trauma can become organized into complexes. You can read more about complexes here, the mother complex here, and the father complex here.

Becoming a mother can kindle both “capital T traumas,” such as a difficult birth requiring an emergency medical procedure, and “lowercase t traumas”—for example, reactivating painful relational experiences of being parented with dismissiveness or intrusiveness. Previous relational experiences can surface consciously and unconsciously after giving birth, stirring complex trauma.

When becoming a mother, present-day trauma triggers such as a difficult birth, emergency procedure, or caregiving demands resembling past experiences can reactivate old trauma memories, even if they were previously processed and integrated. Feeling “dysregulated” or “triggered” often means a complex has been activated. Carl Jung observed, “The complex is not under the control of the will...and possesses the quality of psychic autonomy...in direct opposition to conscious tendencies: it forces itself tyrannically upon the conscious mind. The explosion of affect is a complete invasion of the individual; it pounces upon him like an enemy or a wild animal.”5

That imagery, pouncing like a wild animal, vividly describes what it’s like to be under the influence of a complex and is perhaps most applicable to the trauma complex. Interestingly, the comparison of a trauma complex to a “wild animal” is used in contemporary trauma work; for example, Peter Levine’s Waking the Tiger, which introduces his somatic experiencing approach.

How Unresolved Trauma Affects Perinatal Mental Health

Research has repeatedly demonstrated that trauma can lead to perinatal mental health problems. A 2025 study by Hanna Grundström found that women who experienced past trauma were more likely to feel depressed or stressed after giving birth than those without such histories, especially for younger women and first-time mothers.6 In other words, trauma can influence many perinatal mental health challenges, including postpartum anxiety, depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and psychosis.

I had a patient who suffered from anxiety and a relentless tendency to scrutinize herself. She would compulsively review her interactions: Was she warm and fun enough? Smart but not too smart?

Her family system was marked by both parental absence and intrusion: Her father was emotionally disengaged due to alcoholism, while her mother was consumed by the demands of carrying the parenting and family load. Her mother’s overwhelm and self-sacrifice had a pervasive presence in her family, manifesting in a “martyr complex”—her needs were subordinated to others, while others often felt as if she lived vicariously through them and struggled with being the object of her resentment.

In therapy, my patient came to understand that scrutinizing had substituted for authentic relating, which was foreign to her. We identified how her chronic anxiety was a safe and familiar emotion that kept her from feeling more challenging or complex feelings. While her trauma complex would still surface, she was aware of her relational patterns and related differently.

Where Old Trauma Intersects With Postpartum Anxiety

Then my patient gave birth.

It was as though everything she had learned flew out the window. The demands of caring for a completely dependent infant, coupled with changes in her marriage as her husband became less available under the pressure of being the sole financial provider, intensified her anxiety and compulsive rumination. Her worries now got directed toward her baby, marriage, and how others perceived her as a mother.

She found herself in a role that echoed aspects of her childhood: carrying the weight of childcare and family responsibilities while experiencing the loss of her partner’s presence and support as he left for work.

In our work, we made space for the parts of her experience that could not exist in her new identity. We explored her grief, anger, resentment, and loneliness about motherhood as meaningful, emotional experiences that had been pushed aside to be the mother she believed she needed to be. We examined the unconscious expectations she brought into motherhood: that a “good” mother should be self-sacrificing and endlessly available. I helped her recognize that her husband’s absence was emotionally challenging, yet it did not make him her emotionally disengaged alcoholic father.

Our work helped her recognize when the past and its unresolved trauma were entering the present, creating space to respond differently. Motherhood reopened an old story. In her analysis, she could begin to tell it and write it differently.

My patient presented with moderate postpartum anxiety that reactivated her trauma complex. Sometimes trauma contributes to other perinatal mental health disorders, including postpartum depression, posttraumatic stress disorder, or psychosis, which has been in the news given the trial of Lindsay Clancy, who has admitted to strangling her children. I’ll be discussing that in my next post.

item.title: Finding a Path Forward After Sibling Abuse
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Finding a Path Forward After Sibling Abuse

After sibling abuse, there are possibilities for healing and reclaiming yourself.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • For survivors of sibling abuse, healing begins by redefining anger and conflict.
  • Survivors may face difficult choices about confronting family members and maintaining relationships.
  • It is possible to unlearn old habits, create healthier patterns, and prioritize safety and well-being.
Source: Matt Moloney / Stocksnap

This post was co-authored with Amy Meyers, Ph.D., LCSW

You can find help that will help move you forward and find healthy relationships, even if this one never will be. Once you know this was abusive behavior, trauma therapy is out there in a variety of forms, and you can learn about your true self, your values, and create a plan for a better life that speaks to you inside. —Testimonial submitted to the SAARA Story Archive

Adults who have survived childhood and/or adolescent experiences of sibling abuse may continue to struggle with the long-term emotional outcomes. The impacts of sibling abuse occur both as it is happening and well into adulthood. Adult survivors often face challenges in managing anger and conflict, navigating sibling and family relationships, and finding healing and a path forward.

Managing Anger and Conflict

For many people, anger is a complicated emotion. It may surface quickly, feel too strong for the current situation, or, alternatively, feel entirely unavailable. As children, survivors of sibling abuse likely lacked safe opportunities to express anger, particularly when family members and society minimized the harm. This minimization invalidates survivors' experiences and feelings. Survivors may also have learned that raising their voices or having intense emotions leads to retaliation.

As adults, survivors may find others’ anger, as well as their own, frightening, shameful, or out of control. Yet anger is a healthy emotion and a necessary part of relationships. Expressing dissatisfaction does not have to be negative or destructive. The problem is not the anger itself but how it is expressed, avoided, or suppressed.

Many survivors also struggle with conflict. Because sibling abuse involves both a betrayal of the sibling bond and a lack of parental protection, survivors may experience conflict as a threat to their relationships. In these family environments, conflict may have signaled danger, humiliation, escalation, or emotional withdrawal.

However, conflict is not a sign that a relationship is failing. It is normal for two separate people with different histories, needs, and perspectives to disagree sometimes. In fact, avoiding conflict can lead to resentment, emotional distance, and passive-aggressive dynamics.

Sibling abuse is not the same as conflict. Abuse involves overpowering, controlling, and harmful behavior. Conflict, when communicated constructively and with good timing, fosters growth. It invites dialogue, deepens understanding, and strengthens connection. Learning to see conflict as an opportunity rather than a threat requires a meaningful shift in perspective. Likewise, expressing anger or hurt need not be explosive or destructive; it is a skill that can be learned and practiced safely.

Navigating Sibling and Family Relationships

Often, anger at the sibling who abused carries into adulthood and impacts relationships with that sibling and other family members. Survivors often face difficult decisions about whether to stay connected to their siblings, and sometimes their parents. Family expectations and/or strains, cultural norms, shared history, the desire for a sibling bond, and pressure to “move on” can create deep internal conflict.

Survivors may shift between longing for repair and needing distance to preserve their physical and/or emotional safety. They may question their own perceptions of the sibling relationship, minimize their experiences, or feel guilty about setting boundaries. The choice of remaining in contact is deeply personal. There will always be trade-offs with the decision made: anxiety when in contact, tension around family events, conflict with other family members, and loss of relationships.

Many survivors choose to confront their siblings or other family members regarding their pain. When this conversation leads to an apology or display of remorse, there may be hope of repairing the relationship. When the sibling or family member responds with denial, minimization, or further abuse, survivors may face the painful decision of whether to remain in the relationship or cut ties to protect their well-being.

Finding Healing and a Path Forward

Whether the sibling who abused apologizes or not, forgiveness may help survivors move forward. Forgiveness does not mean accepting the sibling’s abusive behavior but rather understanding their emotional limitations. It often requires mourning the loss of a healthy, supportive sibling relationship that should have existed, or at least was hoped for.

Forgiveness also does not mean reconciliation. It does not require renewed access, trust, or a continued relationship. While it does not excuse or condone what happened, it may involve letting go of the hope that the past could have been different or that the sibling who caused harm will become the person the survivor needed them to be.

Ultimately, the work belongs to the survivor, not the sibling who abused them. It is about reclaiming the right to make choices based on one's own needs rather than the demands or expectations of others. Whether through reconciliation, structured distance, or estrangement, healing rests in the survivor’s right to choose safety and to put themselves first.

The family patterns that were present in childhood often continue. Sibling abuse can shape patterns that survivors later reenact in friendships, intimate relationships, and professional settings, such as prioritizing others’ needs, fearing conflict or rejection, people-pleasing, struggling to trust others, or withdrawing emotionally. These responses are adaptive strategies that were once helpful for survival, and they can be overcome.

Although patterns of sibling abuse can linger across time, they do not define a survivor’s future. With awareness, support, and intentional boundary-setting, survivors can learn to make choices about family relationships that emphasize self-preservation and cultivate adult connections rooted in mutual respect.

Survivors often benefit from repeated, compassionate reminders that challenge long-standing patterns of self-doubt and self-neglect, such as:

  • You matter.
  • Your experiences are real, even if they were minimized or ignored.
  • Share yourself with others. You deserve to use your voice.
  • It’s OK to define yourself outside of your sibling’s narrative of you.
  • You can miss your sibling and still recognize that the relationship is not safe or healthy for you.
  • Distance can be a form of self-protection, not punishment.
  • Experiencing grief for the relationship you wanted is an understandable, realistic feeling.

Amy Meyers, Ph.D., LCSW, is a professor at Molloy University, a psychotherapist, and an expert on sibling abuse.

item.title: When Should You Review Your Life?
item.description:
Identity

When Should You Review Your Life?

You might not want to wait for a thoughtful life review.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Life review can yield complicated emotional and cognitive results.
  • With support, a review late in life or nearing end of life can enhance psychological well-being.
  • Research reveals valuable benefits of life review also for young adults.
Source: Image by Krystine I. Batcho

When you hear “life review,” you might think of an older person thinking back over their lifetime, remembering events and experiences that stand out as special or important. Or you might think of someone replaying key life events as they confront the impending end of their life or in the wake of surviving a near-death experience. Many accounts have documented life review in circumstances involving aging or nearing the end of life. Being acutely aware of one’s mortality can prod one to look back, as looking forward can feel frightening or futile. Looking back can be comforting or unsettling, depending in part on what is found while searching the contents of one’s life. The impact of a life review can also depend upon how the search is done. When looking through a cluttered attic for a specific item, such as an old toy, one might not notice at all the myriad other things—some valuable, others worthless—that fill the space.

Is a life review helpful for everyone?

Early research highlighted the different outcomes that are possible when life review occurs as a natural part of aging. Review is more common among those who perceive death as more proximal. For many, it is beneficial as it can be cathartic and meaningful. It can help put regrets and feelings of guilt somewhat to rest as they are viewed within the broader context of an entire life history. On the other hand, when there are many unresolved conflicts, regrets, and pieces of unfinished business, an overall life review can contribute to depression, anxiety, and feelings of hopelessness or despair. Individuals who habitually worry, ruminate, or become obsessed with unhappy thoughts when reminiscing are less likely to benefit from life review and are more likely to find it counterproductive.

Life review can promote psychological well-being.

To maximize positive outcomes and minimize the risk of negative impacts, psychology has developed structured approaches to therapeutic life review and incorporated them into interventions to improve psychological well-being in aging and coping with mortality salience. Research has shown that structured life review can improve satisfaction with one’s life. Overall, hindsight can help a person understand negative events within the context of motivations, efforts, successes, and accomplishments. Positive memories, especially those related to personal interactions with those who were or have been important in one’s life, can also strengthen resistance to depression. Even sad memories, such as the death of loved ones, can be instructive or comforting when they revive positive memories of a lifetime of emotional support within a network of close relationships. A meaningful pattern can emerge from a kaleidoscope of ups and downs over a lifetime and help one focus on the meaning and purpose of one’s life.

Early life review can inform the choices we make now.

The potential benefits of life review make one wonder whether one needs to wait until late in life to engage in such reflection. Why not indulge at any point in life? Would life review be equally valuable, or perhaps even more helpful, sooner in life? There would be time to apply the lessons learned earlier in life and avoid the futile feeling of wishing one had had profound insights when time has run out near the end. It is not obvious, of course, that early life review would be productive. There may be fewer instances of noteworthy accomplishments or positive events to offset disappointments or regrets. Youth is generally thought of as the ascendancy in life, a trajectory upward and forward. Looking back is often conceptualized as what one does when little is left ahead to look forward to.

Life review for young adults.

Recent research has begun to explore the potential value of life review among younger adults. Young adults recognize reminiscence as useful in understanding their identity and defining who they are. A study of life review by college students revealed improved self-acceptance and environmental mastery, that is, the ability to manage the demands of daily life, take advantage of growth opportunities, and choose or create contexts suited to one’s personal needs and values. Another study of college students reported that short-term life review elevated mood, and longer-term life review over several weeks led to improved mental health scores, reflecting enhanced psychological well-being.

Maximizing the benefits of life review.

Considering the path that has brought you to this point in life can be a valuable exercise. At critical times in life, often points of transition from one life stage to the next, one career to another, or one lifestyle to a new one, a thoughtful review can yield insights that will help guide the next steps in pursuit of psychological wellness. Research suggests that formal review within a counseling setting is likely to yield the most promising benefits. Less formal reflection is more likely to be helpful when it occurs in a context of sharing and social support. Sharing thoughts and memories with close family and friends can help you stay on track to recognize the positive and to interpret the negative with self-compassion and within a redemptive trajectory. If you find your review depressing rather than enlightening or uplifting, reach out to your social network for support, or use professional resources. With an optimistic orientation, caring support, and wise guidance, a life review at a strategic point can reinvigorate self-affirmation, meaning and purpose, and clarity of direction moving forward.

item.title: What Can I Do When My Child Continues to Reject Me?
item.description:
Family Dynamics

What Can I Do When My Child Continues to Reject Me?

A parent's readiness for reconciliation does not mean the child will be ready.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Minor and adult children of gray divorce feel seen and respected when parents honor their boundaries.
  • What a child experiences during and after a divorce can cause relationship wounds.
  • A heartfelt apology doesn't always bring reconciliation.
Jerrod leaves the door open for Madeleine
Source: Mibernaa/Pexels

This is the last post in a series. Click here for the previous post.

Gray divorce refers to couples 50 and older ending their marriage. Today, almost 40 percent of U.S. adults divorcing are 50 or older. Some have minor and adult children.

Jerrod and Friede, my therapy dog, sat on the loveseat in my office. Friede snuggled into Jerrod's right side, her upper body glued to the right side of his chest, as her head rested softly against his neck. Jerrod's right arm circled her to pull her closer, and he began.

"I'm so glad you have Friede. She is exceptionally intuitive. Look at how she is snuggled onto literally half of my body. She senses how nervous I am to hear from you what Madeleine's therapist told you after she and Madeleine read my apology letter. Is it good news or bad news?"

"Well, it's both," I said and paused, waiting for Jerrod to absorb my reply.

"OK. Let's hear it."

"Her therapist helped her write a letter of response to you. She said you can have a copy of it if you want. Do you want me to read it to you?"

"Yes."

I read slowly and compassionately, glancing up to check in with him.

"Dear Dad,

"I would not have written this letter except that Dr. Barkley and Mom encouraged me, saying it would help with my healing. Frankly, I'm not sure my healing is attainable.

"I appreciate your effort and time in writing the apology, and that you took responsibility for your actions and their effect on me, Mom, and Jack, who was only nine years old. I acknowledge your commitment to help me somewhat financially. I know that Mom has kept you updated about me, and I have nothing to add.

"Given your inability to be honest with us since I was six years old, I can't trust you at this point in my life. Six years ago, you blew our family apart while thinking only of yourself, and you continued to think only of yourself.

"I have spent all my high-school years and half of my four years of college trying to work through the shock and devastation you caused. I could write many books about what it has felt like and still feels like. I've questioned everything I thought was real: Who our family was. Who the person I called 'Dad' was. Who I am.

"Your repeated, overwhelming disrespect of me was to ignore every boundary I attempted to set, beginning when I was almost 14. I'm not going to name all those attempts. Dr. Barkley and your therapist have my written permission to talk.

"Destroying the family I loved and needed, you left me without an emotional rudder that a father could provide. You vanished. Mom was overwhelmed and did the best she could to support Jack and me, while all three of us struggled with all the losses. This is where I suffered the first wound. Your refusal to honor my boundaries during the last six years was my second wound. My estrangement from you was my final boundary.

"Dr. Barkley helped me tone down this letter. I refused to let her send it to your therapist unless I could write what I've included here."

As tears slowly trickled down his cheeks, Jerrod sat as stiff as a statue. "What now?" he said.

"What do you understand Madeleine meant by her first and second wounds?"

"She cannot trust me because I lied to her, her mom, and her brother by having affairs and subsequently causing the divorce. She thinks I destroyed the family and that was her first wound. Her second wound came when I didn't respect her boundaries about not entering her room uninvited after her mom and I separated. I continued texting, emailing, and calling her when she said she didn't want me to. I tried to push her to understand what I wanted rather than hear and respect her feelings, needs, and desires.

"How does this help me? I already knew this, and my pain is still so deep."

"Again, I want to acknowledge and validate the work you have done in your therapy to arrive at where you are right now, Jerrod. I agree that you 'know all this.' There is a difference between knowing, understanding, and accepting with compassion for yourself and Madeleine.

"Dr. Barkley and I have discussed what Madeleine shared with her in their work together. It's important that you understand that at almost 14, Madeleine was at a crucial developmental stage. She quickly became emotionally overwhelmed by the crisis she and her family were experiencing, while she was also navigating the ever-changing challenges of early adolescence and asking you to respect her boundaries. Over the ensuing years, she became emotionally exhausted with you disregarding her repeated attempts to set boundaries. Finally, she was unwilling or unable to risk another injury from you."

"Thanks for explaining all that."

"How does the assignment from our previous session to read about Radical Acceptance help you with what you learned today?"

Jerrod closed his eyes, took several slow, deep breaths, and replied. "I was in control of beginning therapy, working with you to where I am now.

"I wrote a meaningful apology letter that included taking responsibility for my actions and the impact they had on Madeleine.

"The healing work I've done does not create an obligation for her to reconcile with me.

"I am not in control of Madeleine being ready to reconcile with me.

"I can't undo the years that preceded her final boundary.

"I can continue to grow and stand at the door I have opened for her. She may or may not walk through the door.

"She wrote me a reply letter expressing what she experienced and how she feels, which was the most she has communicated with me in the past six years."

He shifted his gaze to Friede as he wiped tears from his eyes. "I'll keep healing and growing."

item.title: Why High Achievers Are Often the Most Ashamed People
item.description:
Perfectionism

Why High Achievers Are Often the Most Ashamed People

The problem isn’t achievement—it’s the perfectionism beneath the surface.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Achievement doesn't always correlate with self-worth.
  • Striving for perfection can undermine self-worth.
  • Perfectionism is a common indicator for success among healthcare providers.

The most accomplished person in the room sometimes carries the most shame. Their achievement is the evidence—not of their confidence, but of how hard they’ve been swimming. Achievement itself isn’t the problem; it’s the perfectionistic relationship to achievement that correlates with shame.

Here’s how it works: When the core belief is that I’m not enough, achievement becomes the only proof of worth. If I do more, get more, become more—maybe the feeling will stop. But it never does, because no amount of external success quiets an internal belief.

It’s like swimming toward the horizon. You finish one stretch, and it’s still exactly as far away. The goalpost moves—because it was never real. It was never really about the horizon. It was about managing the feeling below the surface. And that kind of persistent striving toward perfection comes with a cost: chronic exhaustion, an inability to enjoy any success, and strained relationships because you’re always feeling the need to be “on,” or sabotaging connections when the other person gets too close.

Achievement doesn’t necessarily correlate with self-worth. Building one isn’t directly proportional to the growth of the other. And seeking perfection may undermine self-worth while driving achievement, creating a spiral that only perpetuates shame.

Here’s what the science shows. Gordon Flett and Paul Hewitt’s (1991) research on perfectionism found that “self-oriented perfectionism” was generally associated with greater productivity, career success, and conscientiousness when being perfect mattered to you, regardless of what others thought. However, “socially prescribed perfectionism” is defined by the belief that others hold you to impossibly high standards and that their approval is conditional on being perfect. This dimension carries the highest risk profile, with greater rates of anxiety, depression, and even suicide when the person can’t put others’ perceived criticism into perspective. Later research clarified that self-oriented perfectionists are not entirely benign. These individuals still place irrational importance on perfection and hold unrealistic expectations of themselves. (Curran & Hill, 2019).

Healthcare providers are often considered high achievers. A review in the Postgraduate Medical Journal (Oxford Academic, 2022) reports that perfectionism is a common indicator of success among high achievers and of conscientiousness, which predicts job performance but is also a well-established driver of psychological distress. High maladaptive perfectionism is linked to cognitive distortions that fuel anxiety, depression, imposter syndrome, and burnout.

As for me, I was oblivious to my need to overachieve, and I had struggled with shame for decades stemming from childhood trauma. Its undertow was always there. Then the COVID-19 pandemic brought a global lockdown, and in that isolation, shame's pull felt newly powerful and dangerous in ways I hadn’t experienced before.

Examples of how unresolved shame shows up in achievement/perfection include a compulsion to people-please, an inability to accept praise after a win, treating criticism as proof of your fundamental inadequacy, and setting increasingly ambitious goals once one is met.

You can be extraordinarily accomplished—and still feel like you’re treading water. That distance to the horizon? Shame lives there, below the surface.

Here’s the question worth sitting with: If you stopped swimming today, would all you’ve achieved still be here tomorrow? Consider sitting with this question for 60 seconds this week. Notice what comes up and name it. Don’t judge. Just sit with it.

Whatever comes up is the work.

item.title: The Medicinal Effects of Nicotine
item.description:
Psychopharmacology

The Medicinal Effects of Nicotine

The potential impact of nicotine on a range of disorders and conditions.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Nicotine (not cigarettes) shows promise for depression, anxiety, tics, and memory impairment.
  • Trials found significant improvement in response and remission rates in depression with nicotine patches.
  • Nicotine's effects on anxiety are dose-dependent, with low doses reducing and high doses worsening anxiety.
  • Studies on Alzheimer's, Down syndrome, HIV, and Parkinson's are small but promising.

Nicotine has a bad reputation. This reputation comes from its association with cigarettes, and the fact that millions of people die every year from the adverse health effects of smoking cigarettes. But cigarettes have been adulterated to be more addictive, and nicotine itself, when separated from cigarettes, is a different story.

Nicotine is a small molecule that fits into brain receptors called “nicotinic receptors.” These receptors are involved in attention, memory, and mood. Because of this, scientists have spent decades testing nicotine patches, gum, and lozenges as possible treatments for brain-related diseases. Although these results are mixed, they provide hope that nicotine may one day be a safe and effective medicine.

Also, nicotine-containing products are FDA-approved medicines for smoking cessation. A patch, gum, and lozenge are available without a prescription whereas a spray and inhaler do require a prescription.

I previously wrote a PT blog about the potential health benefits of nicotine. But after a reader provided me with additional information, I decided to take a deeper look. And here’s what I found.

Nicotine and Depression

Multiple small studies have shown improvement in depression following treatment with nicotine patches. For example, in a 2018 trial, 15 older adults with depression who had never smoked wore nicotine patches (up to 21 mg/day for 12 weeks). Most got much better, and more than half went into remission. A larger 2024 follow-up study of 29 patients found similar results when nicotine patches (up to 21 mg/day) were added to regular antidepressants. Approximagely 76% of patients responded and 59% went into remission. But both studies were “open-label,” meaning a placebo wasn’t used for comparison. But these results showed that improvement with nicotine was more than double the typical placebo rate (placebo response rate 35-40% and remission rate 20-30%).

Not all studies support these findings. An earlier trial found quick improvement also, but the benefits were reported to decrease within days, and the authors warned that nicotine patches “are not recommended” for treating depression. But wait a minute. This study of 12 patients used a slightly lower dose (17.5 mg), and only treated people with patches for 4 days. It seems to me that a trial using a lower dose and only treating for 4 days is hardly sufficient to claim that nicotine patches “are not recommended.”

Nicotine and Anxiety

A review of nicotine receptors reported that these receptors help regulate mood and anxiety. In a study using mice, low doses of nicotine calmed anxiety while higher doses made it worse. Another review also found nicotine can reduce or increase anxiety, depending on the dose. This study also found the type of anxiety and possibly genetics can influence the effects of nicotine on anxiety.

Nicotine and Memory Decline Associated with Down Syndrome

People with Down syndrome have a very high risk of developing memory decline as they age. Two small studies from 2000 and 2001 involving adults with Down syndrome applied a 5 mg nicotine patch once and then measured attention. Both found modest improvements in attention and processing speed. However, each study included only 5 to 8 people, so the findings do not prove nicotine improves attention.

Nicotine and HIV

People living with HIV can develop memory and thinking problems, called “HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder” or HAND. A 2025 review suggests nicotine protects brain cells by reducing inflammation. Also, a study found that nicotine reduced memory impairment in rats that were genetically engineered to carry HIV proteins. However, human evidence remains inconsistent.

Nicotine, Alzheimer's Disease and Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI)

A trial in 8 Alzheimer's patients found nicotine patches (5-10 mg/day) applied for 4 weeks improved attention but not memory. A Cochrane review, which is typically the gold standard for summarizing medical evidence, concluded there’s no trial evidence that nicotine treats Alzheimer’s disease. But let me add something here. The authors of this review looked at only 1 study of 8 patients (the study referenced above) and concluded that there is “No evidence of the efficacy of nicotine for Alzheimer's disease.” A single study of 8 patients lasting only 4 weeks using a low dose of daily nicotine found improved attention but not memory. This hardly seems like a reason to discourage further exploration of this potential treatment.

A 2012 pilot trial of 74 people with mild cognitive impairment found six months of nicotine patches noticeably improved attention and memory. Researchers were hopeful enough to run a much bigger follow-up, the MIND trial, testing nearly 350 people for two full years. People wore a patch up to 21 mg/day for 16 hours/day. The results showed no significant benefit for memory. However, nearly half (160 participants) dropped out and did not complete the study.

Nicotine and Tourette's Syndrome

Some of the more encouraging results come from Tourette's syndrome. In one small study, chewing nicotine gum reduced tics in patients already taking a standard medication (haloperidol). Another study found 20 mg of nicotine applied as a patch for just 2 days cut tic severity in half, with benefits lasting up to four weeks. Nicotine is now viewed as a potential treatment for Tourette's syndrome.

Nicotine patches (up to 22 mg/day) were found to help people with ulcerative colitis. In young adults with ADHD, a single nicotine dose (7 mg for 45 minutes) improved cognitive performance. In schizophrenia, a review of 29 studies found a single dose of nicotine improved attention, working memory, and executive functions. Several studies have shown improvement in Parkinson's disease symptoms following nicotine administration. These can be viewed here, here, here, here, and here.

Nicotine Isn't Risk-Free

None of this means nicotine is safe to use casually. A large review found that nicotine, especially high doses, can be associated with significant side effects. However, another study found nicotine patches were safe for people with heart disease when used for two weeks. Side effects of nicotine may include nausea, insomnia, and skin irritation.

The Bottom Line

Nicotine is an interesting chemical. It can sharpen attention and reduce symptoms of depression, anxiety, tics, colitis, memory impairment, ADHD, and Parkinson’s disease. Additional studies are needed to explore the potential benefits of nicotine, and to determine the appropriate dose range for this medicine.

item.title: Back to School Teen Social Scene
item.description:
Adolescence

Back to School Teen Social Scene

How parents can support adolescents at the start of a new school year.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Each new school year brings social adjusting.
  • Navigating teen social dynamics can be emotional.
  • Parents play an important support role.
Social Scene Start of School
Source: AI generated

As August concludes, many young people lament the return to another school year. Amidst readying themselves for the academic pressures of high school or college, they must also prepare for what tends to be a social shuffling of sorts, with new alliances, proximate friendships, and budding or broken romances. Whether they are extroverts ready to dive in or socially reticent, navigating a dynamic social landscape can feel like riding an emotional rollercoaster.

For caring adults who love and feel invested in their kids’ well-being, it is hard to be a passive observer. There are ways parents can play a supportive role without riding the coaster alongside them.

Developmental Considerations

For parents of younger teens, observe their social interactions, both in person and online. Allow them to take their own steps to build strong social connections or avert negative peer influences. Practicing independently with parents close by sets them up for the next stage.

As teens get older, parents observe fewer of their social interactions. By then, you want your teen to feel comfortable coming to you for support or guidance when there are relational snags—and there will be. When teens can trust adults to honor their autonomy, they are more likely to engage in thoughtful discussions and value adult guidance.

For young adults, parents and other caring adults become sounding boards, helping them to reflect on their values and priorities so they can align their relationships with what feels truly meaningful for them.

Know Your Teen’s Temperament

We may expect that all young people are dying to ditch their parents and be with their friends, though not all teens are wired to socialize in the same way or at the same pace as others. These fixed qualities do not mean they cannot learn to practice skills for which they are less inclined. It just means those skills may feel more effortful.

Whether your teen is a hesitant introvert or ravenous social extrovert, finding what motivates them can help encourage learning skills outside their comfort zones. Engaging with peers in the context of a particular interest, learning a new skill, or pursuing future post-high-school aspirations can inspire social reticence. Remind socially active teens that their plans may be contingent on tending to other responsibilities and commitments, such as academics and family time. Help them achieve their goals to get along in the world while staying true to their authentic needs.

Be Kind to Their Pack

Whether you like their friends or are skeptical, adolescent social culture is complex, and your teen’s motivations for different friendships may be hard to understand. Given that they spend six hours a day, five days a week out of your sight and with their peers, they are going to connect with these friends with or without your endorsement.

Welcoming teens into your home and showing kindness, generosity (food), and warmth gives you a front-row glimpse into your teen’s social world. Offering to drive to or from events when the whole pack piles in your car can be a treasure trove of dish. These gestures are incredibly valuable and will serve you well when you have future opportunities for meaningful conversation and to offer guidance.

Be careful not to badmouth their friends or express judgments; it sends a signal not to share in the future. It may also motivate them to engage with that friend out of sight, leaving a blind spot for parents.

Highlight Respect

To teach and expect respect, it must be given. We want our young people to be treated with respect by peers and to assert their own limits when they are not feeling respected. Model this with them and their peer group, no matter how disagreeable a particular peer may be. It may actually allow for more open lines of communication when parents are worried.

Barring a relationship in which there may be severe verbal or any physical abuse, try to allow your teen to play that relationship to its authentic end while you are there to support them. Their own experiences are most powerful to shape their future decisions and find those relationships they can truly value.

Be Real With Concerns

When things go wrong, support may initially be best delivered with a calm, compassionate presence. This will require a heavy-lift parenting tool: urge resisting. When teens hurt, parental protective instincts kick in. Be there for them and, when they are receptive, start with questions to assess how they feel and what they are thinking about the situation, such as, “That is a really hard situation. Have you thought about how you want to handle it?”

This is a great way to lead into a conversation where you may be able to offer ideas if they are not sure how to respond or what they want to do, like a menu of relational options from which they can choose, combine, or identify a “special order” response they may not otherwise have thought of. When autonomy is respected, teens tend to be more open to hearing parents’ honest concerns. Be sure to follow up with interest in how the situation resolves.

If there are situations that pose a threat, are developmentally inappropriate, or are at odds with family values, asserting honest limits may be needed. Limits defined by respecting how teens feel about that limit, offering alternative, appropriate options while holding the line, can grease the wheels for compliance. Be sure any limits asserted have a reasonable consequence that can realistically be applied if crossed. Empty or inconsistent threats can reinforce distrust.

Accept Their Choices

Parents will not agree with every choice that young people make. When these choices are differences in preference, such as signing up for a different class than recommended, spending time with a questionable romantic interest, or deciding not to pursue a previous extracurricular activity, it is appropriate for parents to weigh in with their perspectives while ultimately accepting their teen’s choice.

Remember that acceptance is acknowledging what is, not endorsement or agreement. When adolescents feel the power of their choices and parents allow enough space for them to evaluate those choices based on their experiences, rather than make choices to prove their parents wrong, teens learn to make decisions that align with their core values and long-term goals.

Be Available

Be available to drive them, help them with homework, listen, offer a comforting snack, or hear about something that happened that day, even when it’s a frantic call from college. This usually happens late at night when parents are exhausted—listen anyway.

Have a code word they can text you when they want you to call and rescue them from an uncomfortable situation. Make it known that you will pick them up any time of night, from any place, if they feel unsafe or need to come home—no questions asked until the next day.

Above all else, and no matter the circumstances, make it clear to your adolescent over and over that you are there for them. In the end, who do you want your teen or young adult to come to in their most difficult moments?

item.title: Is "Mercy Sex" Such a Bad Thing?
item.description:
Sex

Is "Mercy Sex" Such a Bad Thing?

Sex doesn't always have to begin with two people wanting exactly the same thing.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Long-term partners rarely want the same amount of sex at exactly the same times.
  • "Mercy sex" doesn't have to mean intercourse, and it doesn't have to mean unwanted sex.
  • A sexual gift can be loving when it is freely chosen and given openly.
  • If we stop meeting intimate needs, technology is poised to do that for us.
Source: Dean Drobot/Shutterstock

I've been thinking about the term "mercy sex." It's not a very appealing phrase. It sounds like someone reluctantly giving in, perhaps rolling their eyes and waiting for it to be over. People bring up mercy sex in my therapy room pretty regularly. They tell me they don't want to give mercy sex, and they don't want to receive it, either. Of course, nobody wants sex that feels dutiful, resentful, or emotionally absent. But there is also something idealistic about the expectation that two people, particularly two people who have been together for years, will want the same amount of sex at the same times. In fact, usually, they won't.

Think about all the other things we do for people we love that we don't particularly feel like doing. We go to family gatherings, load the dishwasher, give back rubs, run errands, walk the dog, and sit through a television show we would never choose ourselves. Generally, we see these things as part of loving someone. We even admire people who are willing to put their own preferences aside occasionally because something matters to their partner.

Why Is Sex Different?

Then we get to sex, and suddenly the rules seem to change. We seem to have developed an idea that healthy sex should begin only with both people independently wanting it, at the same time and with roughly the same enthusiasm. But why should that always be the standard?

I'm not talking about sex that feels painful, intrusive, or coercive. I'm talking about something much more ordinary. One person is sexually interested. The other is not particularly turned on at that moment, but loves their partner and wants to give them something that matters to them.

And that "something" doesn't have to be intercourse. It could be holding them while they pleasure themselves, adding a happy ending to a massage, or reading something erotic to them. There are many ways to participate in a partner's sexual experience without pretending that you happen to be feeling exactly what they are feeling. This is where I think we lose an important distinction. Sometimes we may not want sex itself, but we may very much want to give something loving to our partner.

If we remove that kind of sexual generosity from long-term relationships entirely, many couples are simply going to have a lot less sex. Desire discrepancy is common. Two people are unlikely to maintain identical levels of desire across years or decades, through stress, illness, aging, children, hormonal changes, work, grief, and everything else life brings. If sexual contact can only happen when desire lines up perfectly, plenty of couples will be waiting a very long time for intimate connection.

What Matters Is How It's Given

Anyone who has ever received a gift begrudgingly knows that it doesn't feel like much of a gift. The same thing is true sexually. "Fine, if I have to" feels very different from, "I'm not especially into it tonight, but I love you and I'd really like to make you feel good."

That difference is essential. Mercy sex, if we even want to call it that, only works when the giver genuinely likes caring for their partner. They may not particularly want the sexual act itself, but they enjoy making their partner feel loved, wanted, soothed, and cared for. There has to be warmth in the giving. If the giver feels used, resentful, or coerced, then we are talking about something very different.

I prefer the term sexual gift. A sexual gift is freely chosen. It does not require someone to override their own boundaries. It can take many forms. And most importantly, it is offered with an open heart.

Receiving matters too. If your partner gives you something sexual because they know it is meaningful to you, perhaps the appropriate response is more along the lines of gratitude than guilt. We accept generosity from the people we love in all sorts of other aspects of life. Why should sex be uniquely exempt? For some people, sexual connection is one of the primary ways they experience closeness. At the same time, their partner may simply have less interest in sex. That does not automatically make either person wrong. But it does mean they have something important to negotiate.

And Then There Is AI

There's another reason this conversation matters now. The less willing human partners become to meet one another's emotional and sexual needs, the more technology will be waiting to meet those needs instead. AI will not mind that you want more attention or more reassurance. And, increasingly, it won't mind that you want more sexual engagement.

None of this means anyone should override their own boundaries or engage sexually when doing so feels wrong. But perhaps we should be careful about defining healthy intimacy so narrowly that generosity itself starts to look suspect. Sometimes loving someone means wanting what they want, simply because you love them.

item.title: Don't Try to Be Interesting. Be Interested.
item.description:
Boredom

Don't Try to Be Interesting. Be Interested.

You don’t have to fake interest if you are in fact curious and attentive.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Genuine curiosity activates learning and quiets anxiety in the brain, boosting conversation quality.
  • Being interested in others is more engaging than trying to appear interesting yourself.
  • Curiosity widens focus and helps suspend judgment, fostering deeper genuine connections.
Source: Uday Veeru / Pexels

A lot of the advice about charisma or communication tries to alleviate the same anxiety — How am I coming across? — and then offers tips on telling a compelling story, making a perfect pitch or a better argument, or how to have a surprising fact or quirky anecdote in your back pocket to wow your audience.

But if you watch the people who are most interesting in conversation, they’re not the ones desperately sweating out an interesting story for attention. They’re visibly interested and creating interest is a lot easier than producing charm because you don't have to manufacture it. You just have to unlock it, and ley curiosity not just improve the conversation but changes everyone's brain and nervous system.

How Curiosity Affects the Brain and Reduces Anxiety

My friend and colleague Judson Brewer has watched this happen in brain scanners. Curiosity lights up the networks associated with learning and insight as the brain comparing and connecting and working produces new ideas. And, it does something else interesting- curiosity quiets anxiety in the amygdala. Think about it: Anxiety tells us to avoid – this new thing might be a threat — and thus narrows the field of focus, and sets us up to fight or flee. Meanwhile curiosity tells us to approach- this new thing is interesting! Now it widens the field of focus and suggests we lean in and learn. Our brains can't actually run both of these systems at once, so when we move toward that thing with curiosity, the alarm starts to quiet down.

And yes, even the alarm of boredom. I was recently at a dinner party with someone who’s business was sand. Yes, that sand, like the tan colored stuff at the beach that your kids track into the house. I thought I was in for a prolonged torture session, but leaned in and decided to ask more questions. That’s when the sand industry got interesting- did you know the whole sand industry is in recession down right now because the glass industry is down, replaced by plastic on most consumer products except for alcohol, but alcohol consumption is way down.

Climate change has messed up the wine industry, young people are using THC and staying in, and its driving up ticket sales for concerts and restaurants which used to rely on alcohol sales to underwrite the food and entertainment. Sand is related to climate, culture, young people, food. Who knew? Maybe sand is interesting after all.

Curiosity helps us suspend judgment which opens us up for more bandwidth cognitively. This is why curiosity it's actually the whole technique for listening for communication for charisma. And if you're actually interested your face does the right thing on its own your body follows your questions come out sounding natural and organic instead of like a furious brainstorm. You can't fake the signals of interest but you don't need to because if you're actually curious there they are. To paraphrase the journalist Kate Murphy, you don't need to act interested and like you are paying attention, if you are in fact curious and attentive. So find something interesting about sand!

The problem though is most conversations start in a way that make it hard. Like with the realization of oh shit, this person in the sand business. Or we have to convince someone of something, or that we’re interested, or assuming we know where a conversation is going. Notice of these are closed down assumptions and conclusions, the opposite of curiosity, which shut down our capacity to listen.

The shift is moving ourselves from “this is boring” to “how could this be interesting?” or from “I’m trying to persuade” to “I’m trying to understand,” from conclusions to curiosity. And not just about their pain points or needs, emotionally intelligent people will smell that coming, but get curious about them, or at least why sand is interesting to them.

Questions to Foster Curiosity and Better Listening

  • How might I be wrong or ignorant here, or at least not 100% right?
  • What in this person’s history might have led them to this moment or perspective?
  • What emotions are running beneath the surface?
  • What do I have in common with them?
  • What could I learn from this interaction, or what could surprise me?

The last question in some ways is the most important. If you finish a conversation, any conversation, and you can’t answer that, you probably weren’t really listening, so much as waiting your turn, whether it’s a dinner party small talk, a well tread disagreement with your spouse, or even a failed negotiation.

Try it

Can you get genuinely curious and interested, even in a frustrating, boring, or overwhelming conversation? Ask yourself those questions above before, during and after the conversation. Practice in a low stakes audience—an acquaintance, colleague, or even a stranger or your waiter. (Just don’t be creepy.)

item.title: Play Is Serious Business: Let Kids Have Fun!
item.description:
Play

Play Is Serious Business: Let Kids Have Fun!

Kids have lost more than 12 hours a week in free time. They need it!

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • When we turn everyday play into serious sport, we create barriers to participation.
  • Recess time enhances academic time, yet we've moved from a typical 3-recess day down to less than 30 minutes.
  • Introducing casual activity into children's lives—both at home and school—is both fun and healthy.

Last week I pulled out my bicycle to ride to work. I live in a wonderful town for biking—wide streets, low traffic, half my route is off-road entirely, and it’s Ohio, so flat flat flat.

I had forgotten how much I loved bicycling: the wide looping turns, the wind on my face. . . . And I had forgotten how fast bikes are. With my short commute, I can make it in 5 minutes instead of a 20-minute walk. Faster than driving and parking and walking to my office. And more ecologically friendly than having my husband drop me off.

So why had I stopped riding? I’ve always owned a bike.

I know that I stopped riding when I lived in Ithaca, a city famous for mountainous hills and crowded cobbly streets. But it was more than that. The big change came when I "professionalized" my riding routine. As kids, we’d run out the door in whatever we were wearing—shorts, dresses, fancy slacks—jumped on the bike and were off.

In the late '80s in Ithaca, riding had become a "sport." The three-gear "racing" bikes we had ridden were replaced with 10- or 20-gear mountain bikes. People changed into "bike shorts" to ride, and biking shoes to fit into toe clips. And of course there were helmets.

I embraced all those changes, but it took riding from something you just did to an activity—something you prepared for by changing your clothes and then changing back when you hit your destination. It was a sport, not transportation.

My equipment got better. I stopped riding.

Historical Changes in Children’s Exercise

I was not the only one to walk or ride my bike to school. Everyone did.

  • 1969: 40-42 percent of elementary school students walked or biked to school—for those living within a mile of school, 87-89 percent walked.
  • 1995-2000: Those numbers dropped to 12 percent.
  • At present, only 10-11 percent of students walk. For those living within a mile of school, those numbers are down to 31-35 percent.

Biking to school has dropped most precipitously, moving from 6-8 percent in the late '60s to 1-2 percent of K-8th grade students. School consolidation has played a major role in this shift, with many more students traveling long distances to large schools, but school drop-offs by parents have been equally important (U.S. Department of Transportation).

Loss of Recess

Although I loved school, I also loved recess. Sometimes we ran around like lunatics—jumping rope or playing tag in all its varieties. We played organized games like dodgeball or duck-duck-goose and kickball and softball. Often, we’d walk around talking or building little toy villages out of stones. Kid stuff.

We had time to do that. Standard elementary school recess times included 45-90 minutes of free time per day, including a morning, lunch, and afternoon recess.

In 2007, the No Child Left Behind Act upped the stakes of standardized testing, replacing recess with core instruction in reading and math. The Center on Education Policy found that 20 percent of schools had cut recess by 50 minutes a week, with many urban schools eliminating it entirely.

Today, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that elementary school students have only 26.9 minutes of recess per day. For us, that was just our lunch recess—and you could get more if you ate fast. We had two others to blow off steam between lessons. Today, the poorer and more urban you are, the less likely you are to have recess.

Playing at Home

I know that when I was a kid, we were out all the time, with piles of bikes in yards and a constant game of kickball or tag going on somewhere within sight. But the actual data is even worse than my memory.

In the 1970s, elementary school children averaged 3-4 hours of unstructured outdoor play on nonschool days. Three to four hours. On average now, it’s less than an hour. In the 1970s-1980s, 75 percent rode a bicycle regularly—at least 25-50 times a year. A large portion now fall in the "infrequent" category, with regular riding falling to 35-37 percent.

Part of that is that children are more heavily supervised—kids are in sports leagues rather than wandering loose or playing in their yard. However, the University of Michigan estimates that between 1981 and 1997, free play time (indoor and out) declined about 12 hours a week.

As children have moved from free or low-cost community sports organizations to highly organized, competitive pay-to-play models, this loss has been most heavily felt among lower-income youth.

What to Do

My social media feed—like everyone else’s—touts the benefits of exercise as we scroll through our phones. Pictures of slim, well-muscled people playing pickleball, or doing aerobics, yoga, or running flood my screen. All of them are dressed for the role in cute outfits made to purpose: body-hugging clothes, matching headbands, and expensive sneakers.

This is where I started my thinking on the topic. When I was a kid, I got on my bike and rode. I walked out the door in whatever I was wearing and headed out to find something to do.

Looking at the activity tracker on my watch, however, I know that kind of unstructured activity is still where my exercise comes from. It comes from running up and down the stairs at work (12 times a day), biking to school (and home again for lunch), and pacing in front of class while I lecture. Just like I did as a kid. In other words, I don’t "exercise." I do stuff. Wearing my regular clothes. On a completely unplanned but regular schedule.

What happens if we help kids learn to do that? We walk them to the playground? We park a little further away from the store when we take them shopping? We shop at places with lots of long aisles and take them with us?

Perhaps we lobby our PTA to restore recess? There is evidence that recess is great for school performance:

  • Reduces cognitive fatigue: Because thinking is hard work, physical activity improves executive functioning like impulse control, working memory, and sustained focus.
  • Attention recovery: Spacing out learning—like breaking for recess—helps children retain information better and restores focus.
  • On-task behavior: Children are much less fidgety after a recess break, again improving learning.

The American Academy of Pediatrics writes in an official policy statement:

“Recess is a necessary component of a child’s development."

Maybe we should take it seriously as something to do. But less seriously as something we need to dress up for, buy things for, and plan.
