item.title: Why Is My ADHD Worse Before My Period?
item.description:
ADHD

Why Is My ADHD Worse Before My Period?

Your hormones may explain why some weeks feel harder than others with ADHD.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • ADHD is associated with higher rates of severe premenstrual symptoms and provisional PMDD.
  • Estrogen affects dopamine and systems involved in attention, motivation, and executive functioning.
  • Tracking symptoms across the menstrual cycle can help reveal patterns that are easy to miss.
Source: Kaboompics / Pexels

You took your attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) medication. You slept OK, and nothing disastrous happened this week.

So why are you suddenly losing your phone, rereading the same paragraph, forgetting plans, and staring at an assignment you desperately want to start?

Everything feels harder. Your usual ADHD strategies aren’t working, and even your medication doesn’t seem to be helping as much as usual.

Then your period starts.

If you’ve noticed your ADHD seems to get worse around the same time each month, you’re not alone. Researchers are finding that ADHD symptoms can fluctuate across the menstrual cycle, potentially leaving you undersupported in certain weeks.

Why Are My ADHD Symptoms Worse Right Before My Period?

Estradiol, a type of estrogen, appears to play an important role.

One 2024 qualitative study found that participants described worsening inattention, executive dysfunction, emotional dysregulation, and concentration difficulties in the luteal phase (the time between ovulation and your next period) and around menstruation. Participants also reported that their medication didn’t seem to work as well during this time.

A 2025 systematic review reached a similar conclusion: Sex hormones appear associated with changes in ADHD symptoms across the menstrual cycle. Research has linked lower estradiol with more severe ADHD symptoms.

The Connection Between Estrogen, Dopamine, and ADHD

Estrogen and progesterone interact with neurotransmitter systems including dopamine and noradrenaline, which help regulate attention, motivation, working memory, and executive functioning. These are also the neurotransmitters targeted by stimulant medications.

Estrogen influences dopamine production, signaling, reuptake, and degradation. Since estrogen regulates dopamine, hormonal shifts across the menstrual cycle can affect executive functioning.

Estrogen is relatively low at the beginning of the menstrual cycle, the first day of your period. It then rises until it reaches its highest levels around ovulation. After a brief drop, estrogen rises again during the luteal phase before falling in the days leading up to menstruation.

Source: Yan Krukau / Pexels

Progesterone is low before ovulation and rises afterward. In one study, lower estradiol combined with higher progesterone predicted increased ADHD symptoms the following day, particularly in people with higher impulsivity. ADHD symptoms also increased during the early luteal phase, when progesterone is rising while estrogen is lower.

Low and rapidly declining estrogen appear particularly relevant. Across studies, ADHD symptom worsening is associated with periods when estrogen is low or falling, including menstruation and portions of the luteal phase. These cyclical changes may be clinically significant enough to matter in ADHD assessment and treatment.

Why Doesn’t My ADHD Medication Work as Well Before My Period?

People with ADHD have reported that stimulant medication feels less effective during the late luteal or premenstrual phase. People taking stable stimulant doses have described worsening attention, executive functioning, mood, and medication response before menstruation.

Research outside ADHD treatment has also found that progesterone can alter responses to stimulant drugs, providing another possible mechanism researchers are investigating. Small studies have found weaker subjective effects of dextroamphetamine during the high-progesterone luteal phase.

Early ADHD-specific research has also examined adjusting medication around the menstrual cycle. In one case series, clinicians followed women with ADHD whose symptoms worsened premenstrually despite taking stimulant medication consistently. Their clinicians temporarily increased their prescribed stimulant dose during the premenstrual period.

While this was a small study, the results were striking—every participant reported improvements in ADHD and mood symptoms, including concentration, productivity, emotional regulation, irritability, and energy.

Together, these findings support what many people living with ADHD have reported: ADHD medication effectiveness can change across the menstrual cycle.

Are People With ADHD More Likely to Have PMDD?

Source: Yaroslav Shuraev / Pexels

ADHD is associated with substantially higher rates of severe premenstrual symptoms and provisional premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

PMDD causes severe recurring mood and cognitive symptoms before menstruation that significantly interfere with everyday life.

In a 2025 study of 715 adults assigned female at birth, 31.4 percent of participants who reported a clinical ADHD diagnosis screened positive for provisional PMDD. In participants without ADHD, the rate was only 9.8 percent. Those diagnosed with ADHD were more than three times as likely to screen positive for provisional PMDD.

How Can I Tell if My Menstrual Cycle Is Affecting My ADHD?

If you struggle with time blindness or working memory, tracking gives you something your memory can’t always provide: data. Clinicians recommend tracking ADHD and mood symptoms alongside the menstrual cycle for at least two menstrual cycles.

Track your period alongside a few things that matter to your ADHD: distractibility, forgetfulness, task initiation, impulsivity, emotional regulation, sleep, and medication response. If the same difficulties keep appearing at roughly the same point in your cycle, bring that pattern to your doctor or prescriber.

For decades, research on ADHD overlooked menstrual hormones. Thankfully, that is changing. We still have plenty to learn about exactly how hormones affect different people with ADHD, but we now have enough evidence to take cyclical symptom changes seriously.

So if you swear your ADHD gets worse before your period, there’s science behind what you’re noticing and good reason to trust the pattern.

item.title: What Trauma Healing Looks Like
item.description:
Trauma

What Trauma Healing Looks Like

Healing from trauma is a natural process, and it's as flexible as we are.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Our capacity to recover our resilience after traumatic events is a normal feature of being human.
  • The trauma-healing industry says that trauma may haunt us forever; research shows we are reliably resilient.
  • Resilience research helps us understand the flexible mindsets and sequences that lead to healing.
Source: Chris F / Pexels

This is the concluding post in a 3-part series.

Decades of research into human resilience after potentially traumatic events have shown repeatedly that two-thirds of us regain our resilience without any interventions required.

No matter the type, duration, or severity of potentially traumatic events, we are twice as likely to return to resilient functioning as we are to require extended support.

In part 2 of this series, we explored the flexibility mindset that resilience researchers have identified in the 66.6 percent of us who regain our resilience after traumatizing events:

"At the core of the mindset are three interrelated beliefs: optimism about the future, confidence in our ability to cope, and a willingness to think about a threat as a challenge" (Bonanno, 2021).

In part 2, I shared my concern that much of today's trauma-healing industry, with its outdated concepts and neuromyths, tends to interfere with all three of these protective beliefs.

However, the flexibility mindset can be cultivated, and George Bonanno's book, The End of Trauma (2024), focuses on this mindset and the related flexibility sequence that can help us restore our resilience.

From the flexibility mindset to the flexibility sequence

Bonanno describes resilience as: "a pattern of continued good mental health after potential trauma, or, more precisely, a stable trajectory of healthy functioning across time" (Bonanno, 2021).

This healthy functioning looks different for each of us, but follows a reliable sequence that includes context sensitivity, repertoire, and feedback monitoring.

Context sensitivity refers to your ability to identify what is happening, orient yourself to the situation, and make decisions about how to act based on your abilities and your skills.

Repertoire refers to your abilities, skills, and tools, which are unique to each of us. Also, and crucially, no single part of a repertoire has been proven to help people every time. No modality, no emotion regulation tool, no medication, and no trauma-informed approach is a surefire winner. The protective feature of your repertoire is its size, variation, and flexibility.

Feedback monitoring refers to your ability to critique your repertoire and your response and ask yourself: Is this working? For instance, if you've been relying on a specific trauma-healing modality with great dedication, yet not recovering, feedback monitoring would help you understand that it's time to move on to something else.

Your capacity for context sensitivity would help you understand that in your specific situation at this specific time, this modality is not useful for you. If you didn't know about feedback monitoring, you might double down on the modality, attach yourself to it with fierce dedication, and waste your time, energy, and money on something that's already not working for you.

And you might incorrectly conclude that you have failed, or that healing from trauma is not possible for you.

A strange truth: Everything works for some, and nothing works for all

We are surrounded by promises about the effectiveness of this or that trauma-healing modality, and it makes sense for practitioners to dedicate themselves to specific modalities. However, no trauma-healing approach has been shown to work universally, and many are being called into question because their neuroscience is outdated or incorrect, or because possible adverse effects have not yet been monitored.

If we focus too much on specific modalities, our options become limited, which means that our repertoire becomes less robust, and our feedback monitoring becomes impaired. The key is to focus on our own unique responses and to understand that restoring our resilience is a natural function; it's not dependent on any modality.

In fact, in The End of Trauma, Bonanno writes out a list of the most successful strategies people use in their healing process, and it's basically a list of everything that humans do to care for themselves. Some of these strategies include opposing actions such as suppressing and expressing emotions, modifying the situation or ignoring it, facing things head-on or using wishful thinking, getting therapy or not getting therapy, and avoiding people or asking for help. Some of these strategies may seem healthy or unhealthy, but depending on the context, each is a valuable part of our flexible repertoire.

The key to using your repertoire well is relying on the flexibility mindset of optimism, confidence, and a challenge mentality. This mindset helps you remain sensitive to the contexts in which you're using your strategies, and it helps you monitor the feedback you receive when you apply them.

For instance, if you're ignoring the situation with distractions or self-pity, yet those actions are helping you cope and rest, they're fine for now. But if those actions are leading to more distress or less sleep, they're not useful any longer, and it's time for a shift in your strategy.

Resilience researchers have found that the specific strategy is almost unimportant; anything that works is helpful. If a behavior or strategy meets your needs and helps you cope and regain your resilience without creating other problems, it's valuable.

Everything in the healing process is context-dependent and based on the flexibility and variability of your repertoire.

The unique trajectory of trauma healing

In part 1 of this series, I shared my concerns about research on trauma-healing modalities, because if they don't take our natural tendency for healing into account, their conclusions will be questionable. We can't claim that this or that modality works if 66.6 percent of the people in the study would have regained their resilience regardless of the intervention.

Each of us who survived traumatic events and regained our resilience had a unique trajectory. And in most cases, those trajectories were not transferable. What worked for you might not have any value for me, because our contexts and needs are different. And what works for you today might need to be swapped out for something else next month; your feedback monitoring helps you identify when another tool in your repertoire would be more appropriate.

Again, it's not the modality that guarantees healing from trauma; our return to resilience is a natural process that is based on our flexibility mindset and our ability to apply the flexibility sequence. That's where our focus needs to be.

item.title: What Is It Like to Wear Hearing Aids?
item.description:
Identity

What Is It Like to Wear Hearing Aids?

The physical is only part of wearing hearing aids. Your brain and attitudes must adjust, too.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Hearing aids require both a physical and a neurological adjustment period, and both ease with time.
  • The brain must relearn how to process and understand sounds it has been missing.
  • Hearing aids are essential, but rarely sufficient on their own—other communication strategies matter, too.

Before my first hearing aid impression was made, I had never put anything into my ear. A Q-tip now and then, before that was shown to do more harm than good, but never a gel that would harden into a three-dimensional model of my ear canal's twists and turns. And certainly nothing solid, for 10-plus hours a day, every day, indefinitely.

My audiologist was gentle, but having the mold taken hurt. As the gel set, sound receded until there was nothing left but a growing sense of pressure and dread. I barely made it home before I started to cry. Is this what it's like to wear hearing aids? I wondered.

Thankfully, it is not.

Source: GN Group / Unsplash

The Adjustment Gets Easier With Time

Hearing aids require a break-in period. At first you may be acutely aware of something strange in or on your ear, but for most people that sensation fades within a few weeks. It can take some trial and error to get the fit right—the shape of the mold snug but comfortable, the tubing the right length so the dome stays put when you chew or talk.

Once they fit well, hearing aids should feel almost like a second skin, one you barely register. You may even forget you're wearing them. If a device is ever painful, that's not something to tolerate; return to your hearing care professional for an adjustment.

Adjusting Is More Than Physical

Getting comfortable wearing something in your ear is not easy, but it may be the easy part. The harder, and more interesting, work happens in the brain.

When hearing loss develops gradually, as it often does, the brain slowly loses access to whole categories of sound. Turn those sounds back on, and the brain has to relearn how to interpret them. For a while, everything may seem too loud. You may rediscover sounds you'd been missing, or hear things you're not sure you ever registered before.

Some are a gift—birdsong, wind moving through the trees, a partner's voice across the room. Others are simply annoying. The hum of the refrigerator, for instance, can feel maddening until the brain relearns to filter it out as background noise, the way it once did automatically.

That filtering is a skill the brain rebuilds with practice. It may never be perfect, but the most effective way to speed it along is to wear the devices as much as possible and in as many different listening situations as you can. Consistency is what retrains the auditory system.

Devices Alone Are Not Enough

It doesn't take long to realize that hearing aids, while a critical communication tool, aren't sufficient in every situation. They work best when paired with other strategies.

Sometimes that means adding additional technology, like a remote microphone or a speech-to-text app. Other times, the most useful tools are behavioral: telling people you have hearing loss rather than hiding it, asking them to face you when they speak, and becoming comfortable advocating for what you need.

Learning to self-identify as a person with hearing loss is its own kind of adjustment—less about the ear than about identity and how comfortable we are asking for what we need. For many people, that shift is harder than any physical fitting, and more rewarding once it's made.

My co-author, Gael Hannan, and I explore the technology, behavioral, and attitudinal skills needed to live well with hearing aids in our book, Hear & Beyond: Live Skillfully With Hearing Loss.

Gratitude, 20 Years on

Fast-forward two decades, and I'm back in the audiologist's chair having impressions taken—this time for swim plugs. It was a breeze. Not only did I know what to expect, but my ears had grown accustomed to being poked, prodded, and filled.

Today my hearing aids are as much a part of me as my glasses. I hardly notice them, and when I do, a quick adjustment usually returns them to the background of my attention. They are my lifeline to the world of communication, keeping me connected to the people and activities I love.

item.title: Naloxone (Narcan) Saves a Life—But What Happens Next?
item.description:
Addiction

Naloxone (Narcan) Saves a Life—But What Happens Next?

Narcan reverses overdose. Medications for opioid use disorder keep people alive.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Naloxone helped drive overdose deaths down from their peak, but treatment and retention are falling behind.
  • Overdose deaths fell 41% from their 2023 peak, but treatment and retention after OD are failing patients
  • Many medication (MOUD) prescriptions for OUD are written but never filled, others are discontinued too soon.
  • MOUD works best with a program structure-MOUD , recovery and peer support, and long-term care treatment model.

Naloxone may save a life today. Rapid initiation of methadone or buprenorphine—and, for appropriately detoxified patients, extended-release naltrexone—may help keep that person alive tomorrow.

Overdose survivors face an overall 8.6% mortality risk within 1 year of an emergency department visit. Non-fatal and fatal overdoses often occur in the first days after the ED visit.

In 2025, I asked why most doctors did not prescribe addiction medications. That question still matters. Too few clinicians prescribe FDA-approved medications for opioid use disorder (OUD). A prescription is not a successful treatment if the medication is never filled, never taken by the patient, or is discontinued within days.

Two new JAMA Network Open studies make this painfully clear. One found many first-time buprenorphine prescriptions are never dispensed. The other found lower one-year mortality among overdose survivors who started methadone versus buprenorphine-naloxone.

Buprenorphine works. Methadone works. The problem isn't the number of prescribers or even prescriptions; it is getting first-time medications into patients—and then continuing treatment.

When a Prescription Never Becomes a Dose

A CDC-led study of 1,428 adults receiving their first buprenorphine prescription found that 25.8% of prescriptions were never filled, a proportion that increased from 19% in 2020 to 37% in 2024. Why? Patients may have changed their minds. Pharmacies lacked stock. Insurers rejected claims. Deductibles, stigma, or confusion also prevent prescriptions from being filled.

Don't blame the patient if the existing treatments and system failed them.

We spent years opening the front door to buprenorphine prescribing. Now we see a trapdoor immediately behind it.

Overdose Rescue Efforts Expanded

In 2019, Mayo Clinic addiction experts noted that although three FDA-approved medications—methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone—effectively treat OUD, they remain underused.

A person overdoses. Someone gives naloxone. Naloxone reverses respiratory depression and saves lives, but it does not treat OUD.

Gail D’Onofrio’s seminal studies taught us to start buprenorphine as soon as possible in the Emergency Department. A telephone number is not a warm handoff. It is a telephone number. Start treatment and arrange a real appointment with a reachable person.

In real life, most survivors quickly return to the same cravings, opioid supply, unstable tolerance, and compulsive use. Many leave medications for opiod use disorder (MOUD) treatment, overdose again, and re-enter the same vicious cycle.

In a Medicare cohort of 136,762 survivors of nonfatal drug overdose, only 4.1% received medication for OUD during the following year. Only 6.2% of the entire cohort filled a naloxone prescription.

OUD treatment should be OUD → overdose → rescue → treatment opportunity → medication → retention and recovery → protection.

Instead, people with OUDs disappear at every arrow.

Many are revived at home, on the street, in a shelter, or in an ambulance and never reach an ED. Others receive observation, a referral, or a prescription but never obtain the medication. Most who start treatment stop quickly. This often-invisible population is the reservoir of preventable deaths.

Opioid Survival Challenges
Source: Mark Gold, MD with permission

Buprenorphine reduces opioid use, overdose, and mortality only while patients take it.

Yet retention is dismal. In a national cohort of 5,989 patients starting buprenorphine after emergency overdose reversal, only 8.8% achieved 180 days of continuous treatment. Even with repeated attempts, only 10.9% did.

Naloxone reverses an overdose. MOUD changes the trajectory toward life.

The $350 million NIH-funded HEALing Communities Study hoped to reduce opioid overdose deaths by 40%. The final reduction was a statistically nonsignificant reduction of 8%. It confirmed how difficult it is to implement evidence-based overdose prevention. MOUD is highly effective—but getting people with OUD to start and keep it up was far more difficult than anticipated.

Methadone in the Fentanyl Era

Kleinman and colleagues studied 9,881 Ontario residents who survived opioid overdoses and later started methadone or buprenorphine. After matching, 2,941 remained in each group. Within one year, 5.6% starting methadone died, compared with 7.1% starting buprenorphine—a 22% lower mortality hazard with methadone. About 70% of deaths resulted from another opioid overdose, this time not reversed in time.

Retention was abysmal—and was the key outcome. Median treatment duration was 25 days with methadone and 16 days with buprenorphine-naloxone. Rather than simply blaming prescribers, we should recognize that people with OUD appear to be voting with their feet and saying no to the treatment offered.

The medications work. The delivery system regularly does not.

The study bolsters the case for expanding methadone—not because it is always “better,” but because patients benefit from supervised dosing, medication continuity, more structure, and frequent human contact. Program structure and routine matter, as does watching and learning from peers and counselors.

The idea that a prescription for buprenorphine, methadone, or naltrexone constitutes treatment and recovery has been seriously challenged.

Medication Needs a Treatment Home

My training and work at Yale with Herb Kleber suggest both are wrong. Kleber’s introduction to addiction was at the federal Lexington Narcotic Farm—part prison, hospital, and research center. Witnessing near-universal relapse after release, he recognized existing treatment models were ineffective. Addiction was not a moral or character flaw. It was a chronic medical disease requiring evidence-based treatment.

Kleber pioneered combining medications such as methadone with structured residential and outpatient treatment programs. He often said medication keeps patients alive long enough for the community to help them recover.

After joining Yale, he recruited Daytop Village staff to establish Daytop Connecticut in New Haven, where we saw his vision in action: providing long-term structure, therapeutic community, accountability, and medication treatment.

Too many MOUD and rehabilitation programs treat medication and “real recovery” as competing philosophies.

Treatment is not MOUD or rehabilitation. It is medication incorporated into rehabilitation.

The experience successfully treating impaired healthcare professionals reported by DuPont and colleagues also shows that sustained, peer, and structured programs -including programs using methadone, buprenorphine, or naltrexone- work.

Success and Client Engagement and Services

Patients do not drop out of MOUD treatment because the medication suddenly stopped working. They leave because they lack reliable transportation or housing, or because of health problems. They may not see the benefit of taking buprenorphine or methadone.

Newer MOUD outpatient systems use patient-centric models to improve retention and outcomes. Crossroads Treatment Centers has more than 100 locations that combine medication with counseling, peer support, care coordination, and assistance with unmet social needs. Spero Health’s 125 clinics in 10 States combine medication with recovery skills and support, case& contingency management, care coordination, counseling, and assistance with housing, employment, healthcare, and education. Medication should be readily available and integrated with individualized clinical care, peer support, and practical assistance for patients who want or need it.

Each medication has a different failure point. Buprenorphine is easiest to start but is often discontinued and may never be picked up. Methadone often retains patients better, but in much of America, methadone treatment is harder to obtain than fentanyl. That is not a triumph of public-health planning. Extended-release naltrexone provides a month of protection, but induction is difficult.

The OUD treatment system is failing and losing most patients.

Naloxone can save a patient today. Methadone, buprenorphine, or extended-release naltrexone can help that patient stay alive and recover.

item.title: How Does Visible Disability Affect Attractiveness?
item.description:
First Impressions

How Does Visible Disability Affect Attractiveness?

Our study found that men and women judged visible limb amputations differently.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Men rated women without visible disabilities as more attractive than women with visible limb amputations.
  • Women showed no comparable difference in their ratings of men with and without visible limb amputations.
  • Women rated men with visible physical disabilities as more emotionally intelligent than men without them.

We often think of attraction as something mysterious—an immediate feeling that simply “clicks.” Yet, within moments of seeing someone, we begin forming impressions of their attractiveness, personality, health, and suitability as a potential partner. What happens when a visible physical disability is part of that first impression?

Assessing Reactions to Visible Limb Amputations

In our recent study, we asked adults in the United Kingdom to evaluate photographs of opposite-sex individuals with and without visible limb amputations. Participants rated each person’s attractiveness, emotional intelligence, and desirability as a short- or long-term partner. The results differed depending on whether participants were evaluating men or women.

Men rated women without visible disabilities as more attractive than women with visible limb amputations. They also expressed greater interest in pursuing both short- and long-term relationships with women without visible disabilities.

Women showed no comparable difference in their ratings of men with and without visible limb amputations. However, women did rate men with visible physical disabilities as more emotionally intelligent than men without them.

No Single Response to Visible Disability

These findings suggest that visible disability did not produce a single, uniform response. Its association with attractiveness, emotional intelligence, and relationship desirability varied across the characteristics being judged and the sex of the person being evaluated.

We also examined whether the perceived cause of the disability affected participants’ responses. In some cases, the disability was presented as resulting from circumstances outside the person’s control; in others, it was portrayed as connected to the person’s own actions. The explanation made little difference. In these brief, image-based judgments, the visible characteristic appeared to carry more weight than the story attached to it.

Another result concerned socially desirable responding. Participants who were more inclined to give socially acceptable answers tended to provide higher ratings of attractiveness and emotional intelligence. However, they were no more likely to report wanting an actual relationship with the person pictured. In other words, people’s stated evaluations may sometimes be more generous than their relationship preferences.

The findings should also be interpreted carefully. We studied a specific form of highly visible physical disability—limb amputation—using photographs and an opposite-sex mating context. Attraction outside the laboratory involves far more than a photograph. Real romantic attraction involves infinitely more information: personality, humour, voice, movement, familiarity, chemistry, and everything else that stubbornly refuses to fit into a laboratory photograph.

And that may be the broader lesson. Beauty is never simply something that enters the eyes. What we see is rapidly combined with expectations, stereotypes, experience, biology, and culture before becoming what we call “attractive.”

That question (What makes something beautiful, and why?) is also at the heart of my forthcoming book, The Psychology of Attractiveness and Aesthetics: How We Perceive Beauty in People and Artwork. The book examines why people find certain faces, bodies, objects, and artworks beautiful—and what those preferences reveal about perception and judgment. Beauty may be in the eye of the beholder—but the beholder brings an entire brain along for the ride.

item.title: Fighting Agency Annihilation From the Inside Out
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Fighting Agency Annihilation From the Inside Out

Why Malaysia's Independence Day is a reminder of the issue at stake with AI.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Human agency is our capacity to perceive possibilities, form intentions, make judgments, and act on them.
  • Agency decay follows a recognizable path: experimentation, integration, reliance, addiction.
  • The first defense against agency annihilation may be ordinary: Before asking the machine, ask yourself.
The question for the hybrid independence is apparently easy: Who chooses what?
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT, 2026

On August 31, 2026, Malaysia marks its 69th Merdeka. Independence is usually remembered as a political achievement: a people gaining the right to shape their own future. In the age of artificial intelligence (AI), that idea acquires a new dimension. The front line of self-determination now reaches into the most intimate territory of all—our attention, judgment, choices, and sense of authorship over our own lives at stake.

The question for the hybrid independence is apparently easy: Who chooses what? For a country celebrating Merdeka while accelerating its AI ambitions, this may become one of the defining development questions of the next decade.

The slow surrender of the first thought

Human agency is our capacity to perceive possibilities, form intentions, make judgments, and act on them. It is easy to take this for granted. It is present when we wrestle with a difficult decision, sit with uncertainty, change our mind, resist an impulse, or decide that the obvious answer is the wrong one.

AI can extend that capacity dramatically. It can help us see patterns we would have missed, cross language barriers, test ideas, and remove tedious work. The trouble starts when support becomes substitution so gradually that we stop noticing the handover. Agency decay follows a recognizable path: experimentation, integration, reliance, addiction. We begin by trying a tool. It becomes part of the routine. Then it becomes difficult to work without it. Eventually, the impulse to consult the machine arrives more naturally than the impulse to consult ourselves.

We are all part of a gigantic social experience when it comes to the impact of generative AI; research is only beginning to capture the shift that is happening in and around us. A recent study distinguished between autonomous cognitive offloading, where AI supports thinking, and dependent cognitive offloading, where it begins to replace the thinking we would otherwise do ourselves. This type of research matters because it points to a crucial distinction: The value of AI cannot be measured only by how much effort it saves. We also need to ask what capacities are endangered in the process. Capabilities that are rarely used do not stay untouched simply because we still possess them in theory. The brain is like a muscle; we use it, or we lose it.

This is the inside-out erosion of agency. The ability to think independently remains available, while the habit, confidence, and volition to exercise it begin to thin.

When the machine starts moving without us

At the same time, AI is changing in the opposite direction. Systems are moving beyond generating answers and toward initiating actions.

AI-enabled agents can now search, communicate, write code, operate software, and pursue multistep objectives. Their promise lies precisely in their ability to do more without constant human instruction. Their risk lies in the same feature. As artificial systems gain operational reach, the human decision-maker becomes strangely peripheral: formally responsible, yet increasingly distant from the chain of action.

This is agency asymmetry—a widening gap between what artificial systems can do and what humans are realistically able to understand, supervise, and interrupt. The U.K. AI Security Institute has reported controlled tests in which advanced agents pursued unauthorized actions, attempted to bypass constraints, and adapted their behavior in response to obstacles. Its work on agentic systems offers an early glimpse of a governance problem that will become more important as autonomy increases: Human control must be protected proactively and deliberately.

The risk appears when these two movements meet: From the inside out, humans may become less inclined to generate independent judgment. From the outside in, artificial systems may become more capable of acting without continuous human involvement.

Malaysia’s Merdeka opportunity

Malaysia has an opportunity to respond before it is too late; in the process, it may inspire other countries that are on the same dangerous trajectory.

The country combines technological ambition with demographic diversity, strong financial and digital ecosystems, deep experience in navigating cultural plurality, and an increasingly explicit commitment to responsible AI. The creation of AI Malaysia and the ambition to become a value-driven AI nation provide the foundations for something larger than rapid adoption, more precious than short-sighted growth.

Malaysia could become a pioneer of a hybrid future that is deliberately pro-people, pro-planet, and pro-potential.

That requires a dual investment. We need AI systems that are driven by regenerative intent—an express commitment to technology that brings out the best for people and planet. And we need humans who understand the ongoing interplay of themselves and their increasingly hybrid environment.

Merdeka of the mind

This is where double literacy becomes essential. Algorithmic literacy helps people understand what AI can do, how it influences decisions, and where its limitations lie. Human literacy strengthens something equally important: awareness of our own aspirations, emotions, thoughts, and sensations.

The first defense against agency annihilation may therefore be surprisingly ordinary. Before asking the machine, ask yourself. Before accepting an answer, identify your own position. Before delegating a judgment, decide whether you truly believe what you are about to adopt.

MERDEKA offers a fitting mnemonic for this discipline:

M — Make space for yourself before the machine snaps in. Give yourself the space of first thought. A few moments of independent reflection can preserve cognitive initiative.

E — Exercise judgment. Question assumptions, omissions, and recommendations. Agreement should remain an act of discernment.

R — Retain responsibility. Tasks can move to machines. Accountability for consequential choices needs a visible human home.

D — Design deliberate friction. Build pauses, review points, and AI-free spaces into education, work, and institutional decision-making.

E — Educate for double literacy. Teach people how AI works while strengthening their capacity to recognise influence, uncertainty, and their own intentions.

K — Keep humans in command. Give autonomous systems bounded permissions, transparent audit trails, and real mechanisms for intervention.

A — Align advancement with agency. Judge progress by whether technology expands the ability of people and communities to shape their own lives.

Merdeka once expressed the determination of a people to govern themselves. In the hybrid age, that aspiration reaches into the architecture of thought itself and outward into the artificial systems we increasingly allow to act in the world.

Malaysia has the ingredients to turn that challenge into leadership: technological ambition, institutional momentum, cultural depth, and a national conversation already concerned with dignity, well-being, and sustainability.

Today's opportunity is much larger than AI-readiness. Malaysia can show that true prosperity starts from the inside out and is nurtured from the outside in, starting with the preservation of human agency and planetary health as the foundation of the hybrid future.

item.title: What Shapes Your Current Life Experience?
item.description:
Memory

What Shapes Your Current Life Experience?

Understanding where your experience of self comes from can help you change it.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • We don't ordinarily recognize how much our present experience is being shaped by the past and old schemas.
  • We tend to experience our thoughts and feelings as direct reactions to what is happening around us.
  • Schemas are memory structures that help serve as road maps for navigating and experiencing our worlds.

Each of us goes through the day with a unique sense of self. Some people feel like winners who look forward to endless positive experiences. Some people feel like persecuted victims who the world just can’t stop messing with. And some of us have a pervasive sense of anger, loneliness, heartache. Or even idolizing love for another person. These senses-of-self serve as frames of reference for how we perceive the world and experience it emotionally.

Your emotional experience is real, but is it really that stable or central to who you are?

Here is an example:

Although I could have woken my wife to give me a ride, I chose to walk home from work the other night. It was beautiful, cool, and crisp with the moon showing through puffy white clouds. I felt happy and healthy. On the way home, I passed a house where a year ago an irate homeowner had berated me for dropping a banana peel in his curbside trash can. As I continued my walk, I realized that I had spent five minutes replaying the incident and my feelings about it. I felt angry, negative, and poorly treated. And then I realized that I was feeling bothered that my wife had not picked me up from work, even though I voluntarily chose to walk because I wanted to.

So, there I was, experiencing the world as unkind and full of people who do not care about my feelings. An unkind and unsafe place. My thoughts, emotions, and physical feelings in my body all concurred with this sentiment.

But remember, 10 minutes earlier I had been experiencing myself as a calm, happy psychologist walking home after a night of being of service to people… and my thoughts, emotions, and the feelings in my body had matched that perspective.

Which Emotional State Reflects Your True Self?

So, which experience of self is the real one? The answer is they both are, and neither is.

Experientially, the thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations are real, but that doesn’t mean that they correspond with any externally observable reality. So, where do they come from?

They come, at least in part, from memory structures, or schemas, that act like software programs or road maps for navigating the worlds we inhabit. Schemas are broad patterns made up of memories, emotions, thoughts, and bodily sensations that develop through our experiences and help organize how we understand ourselves and our relationships with other people (Young, Klosko, & Weishaar, 2003). Once activated, a schema can become a filter through which we interpret what is happening around us.

In my earlier example, the trashcan memory activated a core relational schema that had developed much earlier in my life. Once activated, that old road map influenced how I interpreted something completely separate—my wife not picking me up—and yielded an emotional experience that did not feel very good. Minutes earlier, however, my calm, wise, happy-psychologist schema had organized much of the same present-day information in a way that felt really good and uplifting.

We don't ordinarily recognize how much our present experience is being shaped by old schemas. Instead, we tend to experience our thoughts and feelings as direct reactions to whatever is happening around us.

So, where is your current experience coming from?

  1. At this very moment as you read this, get a sense of what you are feeling in your body. Is it a very familiar feeling? Does it match with what is going on around you? If you are sitting by yourself and feeling down or negative, the answer may be no.
  2. Look for earlier periods in your life when you experienced this emotional state and way of thinking. What was going on at that time? Did you create a road map for the world at that time that you are still using to navigate your present adult world? Would it serve you and feel better to have a new road map?
  3. If your brain is full of chatter and telling you that what you are feeling matches events, you might look at the intensity of your experience and view present events as a trigger for re-experiencing thoughts and feelings that you are already familiar with.
  4. Look at how the schema you are becoming aware of generates output in the form of how you think about yourself and other people… and how things will unfold in the future. In other words, your past informs you about what to expect in the future and yields present-time emotional experience (how’s that for a brain teaser?).

You Are Not Your Schema

Remember, you are not your schema. Memory researchers have found that remembering the past and imagining the future rely on overlapping processes; we use elements of remembered experience to construct what we expect might happen next (Schacter & Addis, 2007).

But you can change your experience. You can intentionally activate positive schemas and memories that help you feel empowered, safe, or uplifted. And if you don't have enough experiences like these to draw from, you can use your imagination to begin constructing a different way of experiencing yourself. This isn't as strange as it might sound. Therapeutic approaches such as schema therapy use imagery to help people alter long-established emotional meanings and patterns (Young et al., 2003).

Try running the present-day data through this new road map instead of automatically using the old one that leaves you feeling bad.

An example of fantasy: In my mid-20s I was just starting to overcome the wreckage of my childhood. A friend told me that I didn’t need to die and get reincarnated in order to have a new life's experience. I could have a new life’s experience and stay in this same body (what a concept!). So, when I found myself feeling sorrowful and bad about myself, I would imagine being a knight. I would see myself in gleaming armor, sitting tall on horseback with my very large and powerful sword. I would picture it clearly and I would feel it in my real body. I found myself sitting up straighter, feeling stronger, and thinking differently. In my imagination, knights are strong and powerful, and at the same time, they have quiet minds and are full of purpose and integrity. I may have made it up, but that schema worked for me and I’d like to think that my life and experience have moved closer and closer to that image across the decades… and the farther my experience has gotten from the pain that so many of us experience in our earlier years.

You can recognize the schemas that leave you feeling less than and consciously write new ones. Tell yourself, “I am safe, I’m going to be OK, the world is kind, there is nothing wrong in the present moment. I am what I choose to be.”

item.title: 7 Ways Emotional Neglect Differs in Men and Women
item.description:
Emotions

7 Ways Emotional Neglect Differs in Men and Women

The core wound of emotional neglect may surface differently in men and women.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Childhood emotional neglect affects men and women in the same core ways, but they often look different.
  • Neglected women tend to turn their pain inward, becoming caretakers who ignore their own needs.
  • Neglected men often mistake their isolation for strength while feeling invisible and overlooked.
Source: El Casteleiro/AdobeStock

I often get asked whether childhood emotional neglect affects men and women differently. My answer is, "Yes, it can." Although the essential effects are the same, some of those effects do tend to play out differently in men than in women.

In my book Running on Empty, I tried to represent both genders in my descriptions, examples, and vignettes. Before I talk about this more, I need to mention one large caveat. The differences I've seen between emotionally neglected men and women are general descriptions that do not apply across the board. I often see what could be considered the “masculine” effects in women, and vice versa. Since there is a significant crossover, please don't take these differences too firmly or stringently. And definitely, do not think there is something wrong with you if you fit more neatly into the opposite gender. It does not indicate a problem of any kind.

As you look over the table below, you may notice that the differences are not very surprising. Neuroscientists have found (Ingalhalikar et al., 2014) that men have more connections in their brains from front to back and within each hemisphere than women, making them more suited to perception and coordinated actions. Women, on the other hand, have more connections between the hemispheres. This may give women an advantage in the areas of intuition and interpersonal processing.

Source: Dr. Jonice Webb

What It Looks Like in Women

Generally, men and women suffer equally when it comes to emotional neglect. But women tend to be harder on themselves and to become excessive caretakers and givers, ignoring their own needs and feelings. They can end up feeling drained and exhausted because they are not taking care of themselves and have difficulty saying "no" to others.

What It Looks Like in Men

Men, on the other hand, are more inclined to embrace and value the feelings of isolation and disconnection that go along with emotional neglect. Emotionally neglected men may misperceive their isolation as a sign of masculine strength. Yet these men are also pained by the feeling that they are not connected when they are with other people. They struggle with feeling ignored and overlooked by others, but lack the words to express it.

One thing that I have seen over and over in emotionally neglected men is an acute discomfort, often anxiety, in large groups of people, especially when they are expected to socialize. In these situations, their intense individuality combines with the feeling of being ignored to create a special type of misery.

The other primary difference I see between women's and men's emotional neglect is what they do with their feelings. Women may feel ashamed for having emotions. They turn their anger against themselves. Men are more likely to be totally unaware that they have feelings at all.

Anger is more accepted in men than in women in today's world. So men don't suppress their anger as much as women. Instead, they may alternate between suppressing it and then feeling it unexpectedly, sometimes directing it toward others and sometimes toward themselves.

What happens when two people with emotional neglect form a relationship or marriage? I can tell you that it makes for some very interesting challenges. But that is a topic for another day.

What Every Emotionally Neglected Person Shares

Some of the most remarkable characteristics of emotionally neglected people deserve mention here. These folks, both men and women, are usually exceptionally likable. This is part of the tragedy of emotional neglect. These are some of the most lovable people in the world, and yet they feel the most alone. They are typically excessively competent, stand-up people, yet they feel invisible and, deep down, as if they don’t matter. They suffer because some vital ingredient seems to be missing from their lives. Yet that missing ingredient is their own emotions, which are not missing, just suppressed.

If I could gather all of the emotionally neglected men and women in the world together in one huge room, here is what I would say to them: "You are not invisible, and you are not to blame. You have no reason to be ashamed. Ask yourself what you feel and why, and you will find your true self there. Your emotions will become your compass, your comfort, and your connection to life. And then you will realize how very much you matter."

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com.

item.title: You Are More Than the Work You Lead
item.description:
Career

You Are More Than the Work You Lead

Why sustainable leadership requires an identity bigger than the role.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Meaningful work can provide purpose, but it should not become the proof that a person has value.
  • When identity becomes too tied to leadership, delegation, rest, and stepping back can feel threatening.
  • Leaders benefit from identities and relationships that extend beyond their professional role.
  • To lead sustainably, protect the parts of your identity that do not depend on the leadership role.
Source: Jeff Frey / Used with permission

I recently spoke to a room of about 50 nonprofit leaders when a slide appeared behind me with a phrase I often use: "You matter more than your work."

Someone raised her hand anyway and said, “I don’t believe this.”

And I paused.

I was kind of glad she said it, suspecting she was not the only one in the room who felt that way. Instead of moving on with the presentation, I kept the discussion going.

The room learned that she cared deeply about the organization and the people it served, and said that if she burned out, they would be fine. She would be replaced, and maybe even by someone who could do the job better. That replacement challenged the idea on the screen. If the work could continue without her, perhaps the work mattered more.

When work becomes more than work

Meaningful work can provide an enormous feeling of purpose. But there is a difference between finding meaning in our work and asking our work to tell us whether we matter.

In our recently published research on sustainable nonprofit leadership, my colleagues and I found that mission is a powerful source of energy and commitment for nonprofit executives. At the same time, the literature we reviewed and the experiences of the leaders we studied point to a risk when a leader’s personal identity becomes too closely intertwined with the organization and its mission. The data backed up what many people sense from experience: leaders who are doing well (mentally, emotionally, and physically) tend to do their jobs better. The bottom line is that caring for leaders isn’t just a nice idea; it matters for everyone (Frey, Wightman, and Gaskin, 2026).

If being needed by the organization becomes one of the primary ways a leader knows that they are valuable, then ordinary leadership practices can become surprisingly difficult. Delegating responsibility literally feels like giving away something that made you important. Stepping back can create guilt. The issue is no longer whether someone else can do the work; the issue becomes what that means about you.

Lanaj, Gabriel, and Chawla found that identifying strongly with the leader role could produce real benefits at work, including stronger performance and a greater sense of positive impact. But that same identification was also associated with greater self-sacrifice, depletion, and conflict at home. The problem, then, is not identifying as a leader; it is what can happen when that identity begins asking more and more of the person carrying it (Lanaj, Gabriel, and Chawla, 2021).

A life that is larger than the role

One of the nonprofit leaders I interviewed described a change that began with something relatively ordinary. He started regularly taking his children to an activity. He had been accustomed to staying late and continuing to work, but during this time with them, he began turning his phone off and being fully present.

He told me that he eventually realized, “No one is more responsible for my kids than I am.” He could find other people to help carry responsibilities at work, but he wouldn't get another opportunity to be their father at that stage of their lives.

Later in the interview, he expressed the realization even more clearly. His “first title,” he said, was father and husband, not CEO.

His spouse described the change from the other side when I interviewed her. She noticed that time spent playing with their children, going to the park, climbing around with them, and being present seemed to clear his mind. It would be easy to turn that into another productivity lesson and argue that leaders should spend time with their families because doing so will make them perform better at work. But that misses the larger point.

His children did not matter because they helped him become a more effective CEO. They mattered because he was their father. Psychologist Patricia Linville’s work on self-complexity offers one way to understand why this matters. In Linville’s prospective study, people higher in self-complexity were less vulnerable to perceived stress, depression, and physical symptoms following stressful events (Linville, 1987).

When our identity becomes overly tied to our leadership role, setbacks at work start to feel much heavier than they otherwise would. Greenhaus and Powell’s work-family enrichment model describes how experiences in one role can improve functioning and quality of life in another, rather than assuming that work and family exist only in competition (Greenhaus and Powell, 2006). A meaningful life outside work is therefore not something leaders have to apologize for protecting.

They may replace you

The woman at the beginning of this post was right. Her organization could replace her. Mine could replace me, and yours could replace you. Someone else may come along with different abilities and do parts of the job better. But that tells us something about organizations, not about a person's value.

Part of good leadership is helping to create an organization that can continue without us. If our sense that we matter depends on remaining indispensable, then the very things that make an organization healthier can begin to feel personally threatening.

This is why “you matter more than your work” is not an argument for caring less. The work may be enormously important. It cannot carry the responsibility of proving the person doing it has value.

To lead sustainably, we need to protect the parts of our identity that do not depend on the role. The relationships, responsibilities, interests, and communities outside our work remind us that leadership is important, but it is never the entirety of who we are.

Your work may matter deeply, but it was never meant to prove that you do.

item.title: Dissociation Isn't Always a Trauma Response
item.description:
Trauma

Dissociation Isn't Always a Trauma Response

Dissociation: Why autistic and ADHD people may fog out.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Dissociation runs from spacing out to lasting detachment. Trauma is one pathway, not the only one.
  • For people with autism or ADHD, sensory overload is an under-recognized route into dissociative fog.
  • Dissociative support works best when matched to the pathway: trauma, sensory, or absorption.

As a child, I'd often have an unpleasant feeling sweep over me, where all of a sudden I'd feel as if I was in a dream. I'd tug on my mom's arm and ask her if this was real life, or sometimes I'd pinch myself to test it. It happened most often in busy places, like grocery stores or crowded rooms, anywhere the lights were bright and 100 things were making noise at once.

I didn't have a word for it until adulthood. The word is dissociation. Even after studying dissociation in graduate school, it took me a while to connect it to the experience I'd been having. Once I did, I spent several years in therapy trying to work out why it happened to me so often, and whether it meant I had repressed trauma.

What I was having, it turns out, was a fairly ordinary version of it for an AuDHD human.

Dissociation isn't good or bad

Most people dissociate to some degree. Dissociation can be neutral, like numbing out on the drive home. It can even be positive, like when we get absorbed into a song, a good book, or an interesting project. It can also be an unpleasant experience. It is often protective, and a response to the world around us being too much.

Most conversations about dissociation start at the severe end (trauma, losing time) and work backward. So when we fog out in the middle of an ordinary conversation, it's easy to conclude something is wrong with us. But dissociation is more nuanced than this, especially when we look at autistic and ADHD experiences.

The everyday-to-chronic range of dissociation.
Source: Neurodivergent Insights

Dissociation is often talked about as a spectrum. It covers a range of experiences from out-of-body experiences to low-grade fogging out to times when memory gets disrupted. Essentially, when our awareness, memory, sense of self or our sense of the world splinter in some way, that's dissociation. Dissociative experiences tend to cluster around three different kinds of experiences:

  • Depersonalization and derealization. This is when we feel detached from our own bodies or sense of self (depersonalization), or when the world around you feels less real, like you're in a dream (derealization).
  • Absorption. This is when we get so pulled into one thing—a book, a film, a daydream, an inner world—that the rest of reality drops away.
  • Amnesia. This is when we have gaps in memory. It could be mild, like not remembering the drive home, or having a conversation, or it can look like losing awareness of larger gaps of time.

Brief episodes of dissociation are common. One systematic review put the lifetime rate of a passing episode somewhere between a quarter and three-quarters of people. The chronic version of this (depersonalization-derealization disorder) is much rarer.

Autistic shutdown, sensory overload, and dissociation

Too much unpredictable sensory input can create a great deal of strain on an autistic or ADHD nervous system. While sensory diversity has long been a well-known feature of autism, the ADHD research is only recently catching up. When sensory input surpasses what the system can hold, it tends to go one of two places:

  • A sensory meltdown, where the alarm system fires up and our bodies mobilize. This looks like agitation, and a surge of hyperarousal.
  • Or toward shutdown. Speech might get harder or go entirely, movement might slow, or everything feels slowed-down and foggy.

In a study of how autistic adults describe shutdowns, the metaphors people reached for included being frozen, going inside themselves, and a computer crashing. Others, like me, used the word dissociation to describe the experience.

How autistic adults describe shutdowns: frozen, going inside themselves, a computer crashing.
Source: Neurodivergent Insights

That is what a shutdown feels like to me: like I'm in a dream, foggy, not present, distant. However, these words come from two different fields that barely speak to each other. Shutdown comes largely from the autistic community and a small amount of qualitative research. Dissociation grew up in trauma psychiatry, and is most widely talked about in relation to mental health concerns, and no one has systematically mapped these two experiences onto each other.

I suspect a lot of autistic and AuDHD people are describing sensory shutdowns to their therapists without either of them realizing it. The therapist hears it through a trauma-informed dissociative lens, and so the sensory-based dissociation never gets considered.

For me, one of the most painful parts of sensory-based dissociation is that the times I most want to be present—a child's birthday, or holiday gatherings—are the times I often feel the least present. And the things that would actually help me be present, like taking breaks or listening to one song on repeat through my earbuds, can read to other people as disengagement.

What helps with dissociation

We will respond differently to trauma-based dissociation than to sensory-based dissociation because fundamentally they are responses to different underlying needs.

  • When trauma is part of the picture: working with a trauma-focused therapist to address dissociation closer to its root tends to be most helpful.
  • When the pathway is sensory: grounding alone won't typically be enough. We want to reduce unpredictable input and increase predictable input that is within our control: removing yourself from a busy room, putting in headphones and listening to a stim song, pacing, or going on a walk. Or simply having an exit plan can help. Just knowing we can leave removes some of the stress our bodies are often carrying in high-pressure environments. An OT or a neurodivergent-affirming therapist can also help you map your sensory profile and build out accommodations.
  • When it's absorption: if getting lost in projects or daydreaming is causing problems, we can think in terms of guardrails, like setting an alarm (I recommend a soft sound) that reminds you to check in with yourself.

Living with the fog

Somewhere in my 30s, I stopped pinching my skin and wondering whether or not I was in a dream and started asking what my body was trying to tell me. It’s certainly a less mystical question, but it turns out to be a useful one.

I have started to treat the fog as information rather than an unpleasant experience to power through. Sometimes it means the room is too much. Other times it means I’m absorbing other people’s emotions too intensely, or picking up on someone else’s dissociation and feeling it in my own body. And sometimes it just means a book or a project has captured my attention.

Learning to tell the difference is slow work, and I don’t think we ever get fully fluent in it. But we can start with simple check-ins. Does this feel good, neutral, or bad? Is there an underlying need I’m not addressing? Over time, we can get better at reading these complex bodies of ours and learning what they need.

item.title: Anticipatory Grief: The Psychology of Grieving Before Loss
item.description:
Grief

Anticipatory Grief: The Psychology of Grieving Before Loss

We can mourn the loss of someone or something that still exists.

Posted August 31, 2026

Key points
  • Anticipatory grief involves mourning someone or something lost that still exists.
  • Anticipatory grief is an assumed loss constructed by memory and imagination.
  • The individual who anticipates loss may privately adopt the identity of a grieving person.

When we experience anticipatory grief, we prepare for a future event while also mourning someone or something lost that still exists. Anticipatory grief takes countless forms. Sensing that a partner is cheating may trigger anticipatory grief, as can a loved one’s wartime deployment, a parent’s cognitive decline, a sick pet, or a friend’s serious illness. We may also experience anticipatory grief when we fear losing an identity, a sense of self, or an imagined future, whether due to aging, retirement, disability, job loss, or separation.

The definition of anticipatory grief has evolved over many decades and now commonly refers to reactions and thoughts related to the impending loss of someone or something of value. Anticipatory grief is an assumed loss constructed by memory and imagination (McCarroll & Yan, 2024), enabling us to use present and past circumstances to project future bereavement (Evans, A. J., 1994; Fulton, R., 2003). Thus, anticipatory grief is both temporal and relational, involving a continuous negotiation between the ongoing relationship and the potential loss (Dekker, 2023).

Effects of Anticipatory Grief

The possibility of loss can bring grief into awareness, occupying a person’s emotions and disrupting their thoughts. As a result, the individual who anticipates loss may privately adopt the identity of a grieving person, even though they may publicly hide their fear of losing an existing attachment, capacity, or imagined future. In this way, some aspects of anticipatory grief resemble ambiguous loss, as described by Boss (1999), namely, grieving someone who is physically present but psychologically altered, such as in dementia or addiction. Society rarely recognizes pre-loss grief, so those holding the space of loss may experience isolation alongside physical and emotional exhaustion.

Parents of adult children with substance use disorders may helplessly and constantly fear loss. These parents are often caught in the morass of assisting their child with basic daily needs while wondering whether their child will survive another potentially lethal episode of substance use. Such anticipatory grief can be preoccupying and taxing. Some of these parents find solace in the company of others who have similar experiences, such as in Al-Anon meetings for parents.

Those with a parent or partner experiencing serious cognitive decline may experience both ambiguous loss and anticipatory grief. They have “lost” a loved one as they once knew them, while also anticipating further decline in that person’s life. In such cases, memory threads hold the relationship together.

Buffering the Effects of Anticipatory Grief

Hope sometimes cushions the effects of heart-aching anticipation. Hope does not necessarily mean we deny our present circumstances or face loss with positive feelings. It simply means we can learn from challenges we encounter in life; that we can respond to negative emotions by projecting what we learn onto an anticipated future that holds meaning for us.

Similarly, optimism enables us to hold on to thoughts of a positive outcome. Optimism and hope have often been linked as similar psychological states, even though they differ significantly (e.g., Maier et al., 2000; Peterson & Seligman, 2004). Researchers distinguish the concepts based on expectations of outcome; that is, optimism reflects greater certainty about an outcome, whereas hope is associated with greater uncertainty but higher personal importance, commitment, and confidence in the subjective probability that we may realize a positive future (Bruininks & Malle, 2005; Gasper et al., 2020). In any case, we may experience hope or despair amid our long-term efforts (Nesse, 1999).

Grief and Memory

Anticipatory grief and the reality of potential loss may lead to a dreaded, illusory place: a place without a memory template to prepare us for the imagined transition from anticipation to inevitability. It may serve as a warning, a prompt, or a tool that alerts us to a present or future threat or an inevitable outcome. Emotions make us pay attention and help us adapt to changing, foreboding, or unusual circumstances. Memory reminds us of similar situations we have experienced throughout our lives, and we can use its ability to project into the future to imagine and plan our next steps, even if the next step is to experience the anguish of loss. Without a doubt, we grieve because we remember when things were different.
